title: S7 Design Notes
text:
Preface
These are working notes on designing object systems with S7 in R, and on the broader programming-theory ideas that make such designs good or bad: types, values, validation, dispatch, composition, documents, schemas, and the craft of deciding among them. They began as private research — a deliberate “wisdom extraction” pass over the S7 ecosystem and the software-design literature — and are published in that spirit: opinionated, technically grounded, and alive, rather than neutral, complete, or final.
A note on register, so the imperative prose is read as intended. These notes braid several strengths of claim, from strongest to weakest:

title: S7 Design Notes
section: How to read
text:
How to read
The chapters build on one another, but each is self-contained enough to read alone. The overview states the whole argument in ten theses. The three parts that follow supply the reasoning: foundations (what kind of OOP S7 is, how value semantics shape design, what semantic types are), laws and composition (where every check belongs, how sum types and dispatch fit together, how to model documents and schemas), and evidence (what real S7 packages teach, package by package). The practice part compresses everything back into usable form: the doctrine for design reviews, the playbooks for a project’s opening moves, and the middlegame for how decisions interact at real scale, including one fully annotated design derivation.
If you read only two chapters, read the overview and the doctrine. If you are starting an actual project, start with the playbooks instead.
Two appendices keep the notes honest: an inquiry ledger of what remains unresolved — hypotheses resting on single packages, version-anchored facts, unresolved tensions, and the evidence that would change a recommendation — and the sources.

title: S7 Design Notes
section: Provenance
text:
Provenance
The ecosystem survey covers ellmer, ragnar, stacbuildr, S7schema, s7contract, quickr, sqlr and its dialect packages, s7x, the R-ArcGIS packages, resultr, datarr/reflect, rtemis, tooey, rapid, typedjson, objectstore, optimizers7 and parameters7, and structr as a deliberate non-S7 contrast — each checked against its current documentation or source in September 2026 rather than recalled from memory. The programming-theory lineage (parse-don’t-validate, boolean blindness, functional core / imperative shell, the expression problem, design by contract, aggregates, and more) is cited in the sources appendix. Mechanics that matter were verified in a live R session rather than trusted from documentation.

title: S7 Design Notes
section: Living notes
text:
Living notes
This is a living collection, and it stays honest by a few maintenance rules: counterexamples get recorded in the ledger before doctrine is amended, never silently; single-source patterns are promoted only on a second independent sighting; verified mechanics are re-run against new S7 releases per the watch list; new playbooks are added only when a genuinely new situation appears, not a new package; and doctrine changes when the balance of evidence changes, with the tripwires for that written down in the ledger’s final section.
Corrections, counterexamples, and second sightings are welcome — the issue tracker is the front door.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
text:
1.1 1. S7 is functional OOP, and that changes what “class” means
Everything in this research folder elaborates a single compact position. This document states that position in ten theses. Each thesis gets a paragraph here and a fuller treatment in the numbered documents.
S7 belongs to the generic-function tradition of object orientation (CLOS, Dylan, Julia, S3, S4), not the message-passing tradition (Smalltalk, Java, Python, R6). In this tradition a class answers the question what is this thing? — its data, its invariants, its place in a dispatch hierarchy — while a generic function answers what can be done? Methods belong to generics, not to classes. This inversion is not cosmetic. It means behavior is organized around verbs that many types can implement, extension happens by registering methods from the outside, and “interface” is an implicit concept: a set of generics that a class happens to support. Designing well in S7 means designing the generic vocabulary with as much care as the class graph. See 01-object-systems.qmd.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.2 2. Choosing the object system is a semantic decision, not a stylistic one
text:
1.2 2. Choosing the object system is a semantic decision, not a stylistic one
R offers S3, S4, S7, R6, environments, and vctrs, and the choice among them is determined by the semantics of the thing being modeled. Domain values with invariants and dispatch needs want S7. Homogeneous vectors that must slice, recycle, and live in data frame columns want vctrs. Ongoing processes with identity — sessions, connections, caches, accumulating conversations — want reference semantics, which means R6 or an environment. Thin interoperability veneers want S3. Real systems mix these deliberately: the most instructive modern example is ellmer, where the mutable Chat is R6 and the immutable Turn, Content, Model, and Provider objects it manages are S7. See 01-object-systems.qmd and 02-values-and-state.qmd.

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.3 3. Value semantics are the foundation; state is an opt-in at the edges
text:
1.3 3. Value semantics are the foundation; state is an opt-in at the edges
R’s copy-on-modify physics makes S7 objects behave as immutable values: “modifying” a property produces a new object. This is a strength to be embraced, not a limitation to be engineered around. Values permit local reasoning, cheap snapshots, honest testing, and freedom from defensive copying. The architecture that follows is the functional core / imperative shell: pure construction and transformation of domain values in the middle, and a thin stateful rim — I/O, sessions, orchestration — around it. When invariants span several properties, updates must be atomic (S7::set_props()), which is the value-world analogue of a database transaction. See 02-values-and-state.qmd.
crumbs: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.4 4. Types carry meaning, not just shape
text:
1.4 4. Types carry meaning, not just shape
A string that holds an email address and a string that holds a layer id have the same structure and entirely different meanings. Semantic types — the newtype idea from statically typed languages — give meaning its own name and its own laws. In S7 there are three carriers for this: a reused property definition (cheapest), a class inheriting from a base type (nominal identity while the value remains the primitive — ragnar’s MarkdownDocument is a character string with an origin), and a full composite class (when the concept has internal structure). Sharing semantics rather than structure is also the deep principle of loosely coupled integration: systems that agree on what data means can evolve how it is arranged independently. See 03-types-and-meaning.qmd.
crumbs: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.5 5. Parse, don’t validate — construction is the proof
text:
1.5 5. Parse, don’t validate — construction is the proof
Alexis King’s slogan names the difference between a check that discards its own result (validation) and a check that records it in a richer type (parsing). In a dynamic language the translation is: boundary functions accept loose input and return domain objects or fail loudly; from then on, possession of the object is the evidence that its laws hold, and downstream code stops re-asking. Constructors normalize; validators verify; nothing inside the core ever touches raw wire input. The alternative — checks scattered through processing code, each function distrusting its inputs — is what the language security literature calls shotgun parsing, and it is both a correctness and a clarity disaster. See 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.
crumbs: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.6 6. Every invariant has exactly one home
text:
1.6 6. Every invariant has exactly one home
Checking logic belongs on a ladder: external schema validators at the wire, parsers at the boundary, property classes for type, property validators for local laws, class validators for cross-property laws, aggregate-root validators for cross-object laws, method preconditions for operation legality, and internal assertions for developer invariants. Each rung may assume all rungs below it and must not duplicate them. The most common validation design failure is not a missing check but the same check living in four places, drifting apart over time. See 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.
crumbs: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.7 7. Sum types deserve representation, and S7 gives you four encodings
text:
1.7 7. Sum types deserve representation, and S7 gives you four encodings
Much of real-world modeling is alternatives: a source is vector or raster or image; a message part is text or a tool call. Flag fields, clusters of mutually exclusive nullables, and stringly typed mode switches are all sum types begging for honest representation. S7 offers four encodings — subclass families under an abstract parent, anonymous unions, enum-valued properties, and discriminator-plus-validator hybrids — and choosing among them follows from whether the variants differ in fields, in behavior, or only in value. The notable loss relative to ML-family languages is exhaustiveness checking, which must be recovered by convention and tests. See 05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd.
crumbs: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.8 8. Inherit for dispatch and substitutability; compose for structure
text:
1.8 8. Inherit for dispatch and substitutability; compose for structure
The classic warnings about inheritance — fragile base classes, implementation coupling, a single rigid hierarchy axis — lose some force in functional OOP, because an S7 parent contributes a property schema and a dispatch position rather than a method table full of self-calls. But the discipline stands: inheritance is for is-a relationships that dispatch exploits, shallow trees with abstract roots and concrete leaves; composition is for has-a structure, which is most structure. Inheriting merely to reuse field names is schema cosplay. Interfaces — sets of generics with behavioral laws — are the third mechanism, implicit in S7 and made explicit by s7contract. See 05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd.
crumbs: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.9 9. Documents are declarative programs; model them as object graphs, verify them at boundaries
text:
1.9 9. Documents are declarative programs; model them as object graphs, verify them at boundaries
A style, a config, a catalog, a query, a conversation transcript — these are declarative programs interpreted by some engine elsewhere. The R package’s job is to be a good compiler front-end: construct lawful documents, enforce the invariants that are cheap and local, and delegate full conformance to the authoritative external validator at the wire. Schemas (JSON Schema, TypeScript definitions, protobuf) are contracts and design inputs, not blueprints: mirroring a schema one-interface-per-class imports its structure while discarding the opportunity to encode meaning. Expression languages embedded in documents deserve an escalation ladder — opaque passthrough, then constructor combinators, then a typed AST — climbed only as far as analysis needs justify. See 06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd.
crumbs: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

title: 1  Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature
section: 1.10 10. Abstractions must earn their keep
text:
1.10 10. Abstractions must earn their keep
Every abstraction is indirection, and indirection has a comprehension price. The layers that pay rent absorb a real axis of change: generic-to-method absorbs behavioral variation across types; a semantic atom absorbs meaning drift; a canonical spec projected into many artifacts absorbs representation churn; a wire-name map absorbs serialization churn. Layers that do not pay — pass-through wrappers, speculative interfaces with one implementation, factories for shapes that occur once — should not exist yet. The practical test is the rule of three: abstract after the pattern has recurred, not before. The ecosystem itself demonstrates convergent evolution here: multiple independent projects (s7x, rtemis’s PropertySpec factories, and property-factory layers in private codebases) grew nearly identical helper strata over S7’s deliberately minimal core, which is strong evidence for which abstractions are genuinely load-bearing. See 08-doctrine.qmd.

The remaining documents unpack these theses with mechanics, examples from the published ecosystem, and named anti-patterns. The doctrine document at the end compresses everything back into decision guides you can apply in a design review.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
text:
2.1 Two traditions of object orientation
Object-oriented programming is not one idea but at least two, and R is one of the few mainstream languages where both traditions coexist and interoperate.
The message-passing tradition descends from Smalltalk through C++, Java, Python, and JavaScript. Objects encapsulate state and behavior together; you send a message to an object (obj.method(arg)) and the object decides how to respond. The class is the unit of organization: it owns its methods, controls access to its fields, and behavior extension means subclassing or mixins. In R this tradition is represented by R6 (and the older Reference Classes), where objects are environments with attached functions and genuine mutable state.
The generic-function tradition descends from CLOS (the Common Lisp Object System) through Dylan and Julia. Here classes define data and identity while behavior lives in generic functions — ordinary-looking functions that select an implementation (a method) based on the classes of their arguments. A method call looks like any function call: speak(dog), not dog.speak(). S3, S4, and S7 are all in this family; the S7 documentation calls it “functional OOP” for good reason, since from the outside everything remains function application and the system composes naturally with R’s functional style — pipes, higher-order functions, and referential transparency where you choose to preserve it.
The philosophical difference matters for design. In message-passing OOP, the central design question is “what objects exist and what do they encapsulate?” In generic-function OOP it splits in two: “what is each thing?” (classes, properties, invariants) and “what can be done, and to which things?” (generics and their methods). A well-designed S7 system has a deliberately curated verb vocabulary — its generics — that is as much a product of design as the class graph. Behavior is owned by verbs; classes opt into verbs by registering methods. This is much closer to Haskell type classes, Go interfaces, Rust traits, and Clojure protocols than to Java classes, and intuitions imported from Java-style OOP (deep hierarchies, God objects, behavior bundled with data) tend to produce poor S7 designs.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
section: 2.2 The landscape of R object systems
text:
2.2 The landscape of R object systems
A short tour, because the decision “which system?” precedes every other design decision and is frequently gotten wrong.
S3 is the lingua franca: an object is any value with a class attribute, and UseMethod() dispatches on it. There are no formal fields, no validation, no guarantees — only conventions. Its virtues are near-zero ceremony and universal ecosystem reach (every print, format, summary in existence). Its vice is that nothing stops anyone from constructing garbage. S3 remains the right choice for lightweight interoperability wrappers, and it is the substrate that vctrs disciplines.
S4 is the formal system from the Bioconductor world: explicit class definitions with typed slots, validity methods, and multiple dispatch. It anticipated most of S7’s ideas but with a heavier, more idiosyncratic API and some deep complexity (virtual classes, complex method resolution). S7 is explicitly designed as the successor to both S3 and S4, built by the R Consortium’s OOP Working Group with representatives from R-Core, Bioconductor, Posit/tidyverse, and the wider community — a genuinely cross-camp effort, which matters because it means S7 is intended to be the convergence point rather than another parallel system.
R6 provides message-passing OOP with reference semantics: objects are mutable, methods are attached, $clone() exists because copies are no longer automatic. R6 is not a competitor to S7; it answers a different question (identity and mutation) and appears alongside S7 in well-designed packages.
Environments are the raw material of reference semantics — mutable bags with identity — useful for caches and registries when R6’s structure would be overhead.
vctrs is not an object system so much as a rigorous S3 framework for vector types: it supplies the algebra of sizes, prototypes, casting, and coercion that makes a custom vector behave correctly in c(), [, data.frame columns, and joins. If the thing you are modeling is fundamentally a column of homogeneous values, vctrs is the answer and S7 is not; re-implementing coercion rules in S7 validators is wasted, buggy effort.
S7, finally: formal classes with typed, validated, defaulted properties; class validators for whole-object invariants; single and multiple dispatch via generics; explicit super(); declared compatibility with S3 and S4 in both directions.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
section: 2.3 What is distinctive about S7 itself
text:
2.3 What is distinctive about S7 itself
Several S7 design decisions reward close attention because they enable patterns that S3/S4 made awkward.
Classes are first-class values. new_class() returns an object that is simultaneously the class definition and its constructor. You call it to make instances; you pass it around like any value; you store it in lists; you write functions that return classes. This makes class factories a natural pattern — a function that stamps out enum classes from a vector of variants, for example — and it makes registries of classes (for round-trip deserialization: wire tag to class object) trivial. Languages where classes are compile-time entities need reflection to do what S7 does with a named list.
The same fact makes genuine reflection buildable in ordinary R code, with no support from the system: because a class object carries @properties, @parent, @validator, and its own @constructor, a tool can walk them and report, for every property, its declared type, whether it has a default or a validator, whether it is required (a constructor formal equal to the empty symbol), and which ancestor declared it. The datarr/reflect package does exactly this — immutable descriptor objects for properties, methods, and callables, with method tables enumerated per generic and S7’s own method_explain() attached as a dispatch trace — and the descriptors are themselves S7 objects, the metaobject-protocol idea realized as an ordinary package. Whether or not one needs a reflection library, the design consequence stands: anything you can state about a class (documentation, schemas, UI forms, audits) can be derived from the class, because the class is data.
Properties have a full lifecycle. A property is not just a typed slot. It carries a class (which may be a union), a default (which may be a quoted expression evaluated at construction — the standard trick for required properties is default = quote(stop("Required"))), an optional validator, and optional getter/setter for computed or guarded access. This is the layer where most fine-grained design happens, and it is examined throughout 03-types-and-meaning.qmd and 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.
Validation is built into the object lifecycle. The class validator runs at construction and after every property replacement. Validity is not something you remember to call; it is a property of being an object at all. The consequences — both the guarantees and the cost model — are the subject of 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.
Dispatch is explicit and disciplined. Generics declare their dispatch arguments; method signatures are checked for compatibility against the generic (a method missing an argument the generic promises produces a warning; a method without ... refuses misspelled arguments instead of silently swallowing them, a real S3 footgun). super(x, to = Parent) replaces the implicit NextMethod() with an explicit statement of which parent behavior you want. Multiple dispatch exists (new_generic(dispatch_args = c("x", "y"))) and, while rare, is decisive where behavior genuinely depends on two types at once — serializing a value for a dialect, converting from one type to another, combining two objects. The special classes class_any and class_missing round out multiple dispatch by matching anything and matching an absent argument respectively.
Compatibility is bidirectional. S7 methods can be registered on S3 generics; S3 and S4 classes can serve as property types (an S4 class via methods::getClass(), an S3 class via new_S3_class()); S7 classes can have methods on S4 generics. This matters strategically: adopting S7 does not fence you off from the ecosystem, and hybrid designs (an S7 property holding a DBI S4 connection, an S7 class fronted by an S3 facade) are supported rather than hacked.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
section: 2.4 Choosing the substrate: a semantic decision procedure
text:
2.4 Choosing the substrate: a semantic decision procedure
The question “S7 or something else?” is answered by the semantics of the thing being modeled, in roughly this order:

Is it fundamentally a vector — a column of homogeneous values that must slice, concatenate, recycle, and live in data frames? Then vctrs, possibly held by an S7 object but not replaced by one.
Does it have identity and a lifetime — a conversation, a connection, a cache, an accumulating log — where two references to it must observe each other’s changes? Then reference semantics: R6 or an environment. An S7 value may snapshot it, but the live thing is a reference.
Is it a domain value — a fact, a configuration, a document, a message, a measurement — with internal laws worth enforcing and behavior worth dispatching on? Then S7.
Is it a veneer over something that already works, needed only so a print method looks right? Then S3, and stop there.

The most instructive designs use several systems at once, on purpose. In ellmer, the Chat object is R6 because a conversation is an ongoing process with identity — you append turns to it — while every Turn inside it is an immutable S7 value, because a turn is a record of fact. In ragnar, MarkdownDocumentChunks is an S7 class that inherits from tibble: the data is fundamentally tabular (so it should behave as a data frame) but carries a @document property and domain identity on top. These are not compromises; they are the point. The systems are tools with distinct semantics, and fluency means combining them without ideology.

title: 2  Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is
section: 2.5 The expression problem, briefly
text:
2.5 The expression problem, briefly
Generic-function OOP has a distinctive relationship to what Philip Wadler named the expression problem: the difficulty of adding both new data variants and new operations to a system without modifying existing code. Class-owned methods make new variants easy (subclass) and new operations hard (edit every class). Pattern-matching functional code makes new operations easy (new function) and new variants hard (edit every match). Generic functions make both directions open: anyone can add a class and register methods for existing generics; anyone can add a generic and register methods for existing classes. ellmer exploits exactly this: adding a new LLM provider means adding a Provider subclass and registering methods on the existing generic vocabulary — no core changes.
The price of this openness is the absence of exhaustiveness checking: nothing verifies at definition time that every variant handles every generic. The mitigations — sealed-hierarchy conventions, defaults that fail loudly, tests that enumerate the registry — are discussed in 05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
text:
3.1 R’s physics: copy-on-modify
R is, at bottom, a language of values. Bindings point at immutable-in-spirit objects, and what looks like mutation — x[1] <- 5, df$col <- z, style@zoom <- 10 — is actually replace and rebind: a modified copy is produced and the name is pointed at it. The @<- form is syntactic sugar for a replacement function call followed by reassignment. Two consequences follow immediately for S7 design.
First, S7 objects are values. If a function receives an S7 object and “modifies” it, the caller’s copy is untouched. There is no spooky action at a distance, no need for defensive copies, no aliasing bugs. An object you hold is yours.
Second, validation hooks into replacement. Because property “mutation” is really the construction of a new object, S7 can (and does) run validators on every property replacement. Validity becomes an invariant of existing at all, not a state you hope the object is in. This is the mechanical foundation for the parse-don’t-validate discipline in 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
section: 3.2 Why value semantics are a superpower for domain modeling
text:
3.2 Why value semantics are a superpower for domain modeling
Rich Hickey’s “value of values” argument is worth internalizing beyond its Clojure origins. A value — an immutable piece of data — can be shared without coordination, cached without invalidation protocols, compared by content, snapshotted for free, and reasoned about locally: what you see at the call site is what the function gets, forever. For domain modeling specifically, values buy you:

Honest testing. A value-in, value-out function is a fact you can check with identical() and snapshot tests. No setup/teardown of hidden state.
Free history. Keeping the old version of a document is just… keeping it. Undo, diffing, and audit trails fall out of the semantics.
Branching. Two candidate variants of a configuration are two values. Nothing needs cloning ceremonies; ellmer’s R6 Chat needs an explicit $clone() to fork a conversation precisely because it opted out of value semantics.
Equational reasoning. Transformations compose as functions. A pipeline style |> add_layer(l) |> set_zoom(10) reads as algebra because it is.

The temptation to resist is making domain objects mutable “because updating is annoying.” The annoyance is real (deep updates in value-land involve rebuilding paths through the structure) but it is the cost side of every guarantee listed above, and R’s replacement-function machinery plus well-designed mutator generics (add_layer(style, layer) returning a new style) absorbs most of it.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
section: 3.3 Where reference semantics genuinely belong
text:
3.3 Where reference semantics genuinely belong
Value semantics are the wrong answer for a specific, identifiable class of things: those with identity and a lifetime — where the whole point is that observers share the same evolving thing.

A conversation being appended to, turn by turn.
A connection or session with a server, a file handle, a browser tab.
A cache or memoization table, whose entire purpose is coordinated mutation.
A registry that accumulates plugins or handlers at load time.
UI state observed by a reactive framework.

R expresses these with environments, R6, or external pointers. The design failure mode is not using reference semantics — it is using them for things that are actually facts. A turn that has been said, a measurement that was taken, a style that was published: these are records, and records are values. The heuristic: nouns that are ongoing processes get references; nouns that are records of fact get values.
One qualification deserves stating as a law of its own, because it bounds every claim above: value semantics is only as deep as the payload. An S7 object behaves dependably as a value only when everything reachable through its properties is itself value-like. A property holding an environment, an R6 object, an external pointer, or a connection is a reference inside a value: copying the object copies the pointer, not the contents, and every “copy” observes mutations of the shared payload. This is directly demonstrable — assign into an environment held as a property through one binding, and the change is visible through the other binding, even after the two objects have otherwise diverged. The wrapper does not immunize its contents. The design consequences: if a class must hold a reference, say so in its documentation, exclude the reference from equality and serialization expectations (two equal-by-content objects sharing a cache environment are not identical() and should not claim to be), or snapshot the referenced state into plain data at the boundary so the object really is a value.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
section: 3.4 Functional core, imperative shell
text:
3.4 Functional core, imperative shell
Gary Bernhardt’s “Boundaries” talk gave the canonical name to the architecture these observations imply: a functional core of pure functions over immutable values, wrapped in a thin imperative shell that talks to the world. The shell fetches, reads, writes, streams, and mutates session state; the core decides, transforms, constructs, and validates. Values cross the boundary; decisions concentrate in the core where they are trivially testable; side effects concentrate in the shell where they are at least localized.
In R terms:

Core: S7 constructors and validators; pure transformations from object to object; serialization to and from plain lists; generation of documents, queries, expressions.
Shell: httr2 requests, file I/O, database and GDAL calls, Shiny reactivity, LLM streaming, R6 orchestrators.

ellmer is the cleanest published illustration. The R6 Chat object is the shell: it owns the HTTP lifecycle, the streaming, the tool-invocation loop, and the accumulating list of turns — a state machine with identity. Everything that flows through it is S7 values: Turn objects containing Content objects, a Model configuration, a Provider description. The values are what you inspect, test, serialize, and reprocess; the R6 object is how the process is driven. Neither system is asked to do the other’s job.
The architecture has a fully formalized variant worth knowing by name: the Model–View–Update (Elm) architecture, which the tooey terminal-UI framework brings to R. An application is three pure functions — update(model, msg) maps the current state and an incoming message to a new state plus commands, and view(model, buf) renders state into a screen buffer — while the framework’s runtime owns the terminal, the clock, and keyboard input, delivering them as plain data messages and executing the returned command values. Everything the programmer writes is functional core; the imperative shell is supplied by the framework and cannot be reached from application code. Beyond UI, MVU is the answer to a question value-oriented designs eventually face — where do events go? — and the answer is: events are values too, dispatched over like any other variant family, folded into state by one pure function.
The test for whether you have the boundary right: could you reconstruct the entire domain state from the values alone, replaying or discarding the shell? If domain knowledge exists only as mutable state inside a reference object, the boundary has leaked.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
section: 3.5 A taxonomy of state
text:
3.5 A taxonomy of state
“State” is not one thing. Separating its kinds prevents both over-engineering (R6 everywhere) and under-engineering (globals in disguise).
Document state — the current value of the domain object itself. Lives in S7 values; changes by replacement through constructors and mutator generics.
Derived state — anything computable from document state: an index from layer id to layer, a count, a rendered preview. The default is to not store it: compute on read, possibly via a getter-backed dynamic property. If computation is expensive, memoize outside the object (an environment keyed by content hash), because caching inside a value corrupts its value-ness — two objects with equal domain content should be equal.
Collection state — registries of named things inside a document (sources by id, items by key). These are just properties (named lists) of an aggregate object; their invariants (unique ids, valid references) belong to that aggregate’s validator, as developed in 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.
Session state — the live process: connections, conversations, event loops. R6 or environments, in the shell.
Configuration state — options, environment variables, credentials. Read at the boundary and passed in as values; a core function that consults options() mid-computation has smuggled in a hidden input.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
section: 3.6 Atomic updates and the transaction analogy
text:
3.6 Atomic updates and the transaction analogy
S7 validates after each property replacement. When an invariant spans several properties, sequential single-property updates can pass through transiently invalid intermediate states — and the validator will correctly reject the intermediate, even though the final state would have been fine. Suppose a class requires start <= end and both must move forward:
# fails if new start exceeds old end, despite a valid final state
x@start <- 15
x@end <- 20

# atomic: validate once, after both replacements
S7::set_props(x, start = 15, end = 20)
This is exactly a database transaction in miniature: constraints are checked at commit, not per statement. The design rule that follows: any invariant spanning multiple properties implies that every code path updating those properties must go through an atomic multi-property update — usually wrapped in a mutator function so callers cannot get it wrong.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
section: 3.7 Getters, setters, and the discipline of cheap access
text:
3.7 Getters, setters, and the discipline of cheap access
S7 properties may carry a getter (making the property computed and, without a setter, read-only — and excluded from the default constructor, since it is not stored state) and a setter (which receives self and value and returns the modified self, enabling normalization on write).
Two contracts deserve emphasis because S7 does not enforce them for you. First, a getter’s return value is not validated against the declared class; you are on your honor. Second, and more important as a design matter: property access must be cheap and pure. The entire mental model of an S7 object is “structured data.” A getter that performs I/O, network calls, or expensive computation silently converts data access into action-at-a-distance and destroys the reader’s ability to reason about cost or effects. Computed properties are for derivations (a duration from start and end, a full name from parts, a constant discriminator), not for laziness tricks.
Setters, symmetrically, are for normalization that preserves meaning — trimming whitespace, sorting a tag set, upgrading a bare scalar to a length-one vector. The moment a setter starts making semantic decisions or enforcing cross-property rules, it is doing a constructor’s or validator’s job in a place readers will not look.

title: 3  Values and State: Reference Semantics, Immutability, and Where Change Lives
section: 3.8 Identity, equality, and testing
text:
3.8 Identity, equality, and testing
Value objects compare by content: identical(a, b) answers “are these the same fact?” Reference objects compare by identity: two R6 handles are “equal” only if they are the same object. This distinction propagates into testing strategy. Value-centric designs test with input/output assertions and snapshots of serialized form; reference-centric designs need lifecycle tests (construct, mutate, observe) and are correspondingly more expensive to cover. A design that keeps the domain in values and confines references to the shell inherits the cheap testing profile for everything that matters most.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
text:
4.1 Three lenses on what a type is
Before designing with types it helps to hold three complementary definitions in mind.
A type is a set of values. integer between 0 and 255 names a set; nonempty string names a set. Under this lens, subtyping is subset-hood, a union type is a set union, and a validator is a membership predicate.
A type is a contract on operations. Knowing x is a Color tells you what you may do: read channels, convert to hex, blend. Under this lens, interfaces and generics define types as much as data layouts do — a “thing that can be serialized” is a type in the behavioral sense even if no class hierarchy says so.
A type is a name for meaning. EmailAddress and CustomerId may both be strings-as-sets, and support the same operations-as-contracts, yet naming them separately encodes knowledge: these are different kinds of thing, and substituting one for the other is a bug even when no operation would fail.
Static languages let a compiler exploit all three lenses. In R, a dynamic language, the sets are enforced at runtime (validators), the contracts by dispatch and convention, and the meanings by the class graph you choose to build. The absence of a compiler does not make type thinking pointless — it makes it a design discipline rather than a checked artifact. Your constructor set is your type system; your validators are its proof obligations; your generics are its interfaces.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.2 Structural versus nominal — and where semantics enters
text:
4.2 Structural versus nominal — and where semantics enters
Type systems differ in what makes two types “the same.” Structural typing (TypeScript, Go interfaces) says: same shape, same type — any object with the right fields satisfies the interface. Nominal typing (Java, Haskell’s newtypes) says: same name, same type — identical shapes with different declarations are different types.
R at runtime is loosely structural: code that reaches into x$field works on anything with that field. S7 layers nominal identity on top: dispatch and property-class checks consult the declared class, not the shape. And a property’s declared class is itself a structural constraint on that slot. So an S7 design mixes the two deliberately: nominal identity where meaning must not be confused, structural constraints where shape is what matters.
The third notion — semantic typing — is the design payoff of nominal identity. The classic statically typed device is the newtype: wrap a primitive in a distinct type (CustomerId wrapping string) so that the compiler stops you from passing a customer id where an order id is expected. The wrapper adds no structure; it adds meaning and prevents an entire class of “stringly typed” defects where everything is a character vector and nothing stops the wrong one from arriving.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.3 Semantic contracts and loose coupling
text:
4.3 Semantic contracts and loose coupling
There is a systems-integration corollary that elevates semantic types from a convenience to an architectural principle. When two systems integrate by sharing structure — an agreed record layout — every structural change in one forces coordination with the other; the coupling is total. When they integrate by sharing semantics — agreed atomic meanings like CustomerId, EmailAddress, FloodZoneClass — each system arranges those atoms in whatever local structure suits it, and a mapping layer mediates. Structures then evolve independently while data remains meaningfully exchangeable, because the meanings are the stable contract.
(This idea is developed explicitly in data-integration languages like Taxi, where type CustomerId inherits String declarations are shared across systems precisely so models do not have to be. The design notes in s7-thoughts-and-notes.md arrive at the same conclusion independently.)
The general lesson for any multi-dialect domain — several external schemas describing overlapping concepts — is to build the semantic layer first (the atoms shared across dialects) and let each dialect’s document structure be a separate, local composition of those atoms. The alternative, modeling one dialect’s structure and treating others as deviations from it, couples you to the dialect you happened to start with.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.5 Type-driven design in a dynamic language
text:
4.5 Type-driven design in a dynamic language
The type-driven design slogan — make illegal states unrepresentable (Yaron Minsky) — translates to dynamic R as make illegal states unconstructable. You cannot stop the interpreter from holding a bad list, but you can arrange that no bad object of your class ever exists: the constructor parses, the validators enforce, and every mutation path revalidates. Possession of the object then certifies its laws, which is the bridge to 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.
The practical workflow, adapted from the typed-functional world (Scott Wlaschin’s Domain Modeling Made Functional is the best book-length treatment):

Enumerate the vocabulary. List the domain’s nouns and the sets of values each can take, before writing any class. Distinguish atoms (indivisible meanings) from composites (arrangements of atoms).
Write the laws next to the nouns. “Alpha is a proportion.” “A zoom level lies in [0, 24].” “Every layer references an existing source.” Each law will land on a specific rung of the validation ladder.
Represent alternatives as alternatives. Where the domain says “either X or Y,” reach for a sum-type encoding (05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd) rather than optional fields with implicit exclusivity.
Let the verbs emerge. Once the nouns are stable, the generic vocabulary — construct, combine, serialize, render, convert — tends to write itself, and methods slot in per class.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.6 Data-driven design, in two senses
text:
4.6 Data-driven design, in two senses
“Data-driven” names two distinct and equally useful ideas, and conflating them causes confusion.
Design driven by data about the domain. Before abstracting, census the actual corpus: which shapes recur across a specification, which fields are required in practice, which enum values actually occur. Abstractions are then earned by observed repetition rather than speculated. A property-factory layer, for instance, should contain exactly the factories the census justifies — the shapes that occur dozens of times — and nothing “for completeness.” This is the rule of three operating at design scale, and it is the discipline that keeps foundation layers small and honest.
Behavior represented as data. Tables and specifications that drive computation: a classification table that generates both a style expression and a legend; a schedule that drives a state machine; quoted expressions composed into generated validator functions. This is the older Lisp/Unix sense — programs manipulating programs-as-data — and it reappears in 06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd as the foundation of DSL and codegen work. Its cardinal rule: the data is the single source of truth, and all downstream artifacts are projections from it, never hand-maintained in parallel.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.7 The wire universe versus the domain universe
text:
4.7 The wire universe versus the domain universe
Documents live in an impoverished type universe. JSON has exactly six kinds: null, boolean, number, string, array, object. R’s universe is richer and messier: NULL and NA (distinct!), integer versus double, length-one vectors standing in for scalars, named lists versus unnamed lists, attributes. Designing a document model means designing the mapping between universes, and most of the notorious bugs live in four mismatches:

Number: JSON does not distinguish 8 from 8L. If a property demands class_integer, wire input and casual users will supply doubles. Either accept class_numeric plus an integerish validator, or coerce in the constructor — but decide once, globally.
Scalar: JSON has scalars; R has length-one vectors. Every “string” property needs a length-1 law somewhere, which is why scalar-ness is usually the first check in any property-validator foundation.
Nothing: JSON can omit a key, or set it to null; R has NULL and also NA. These are up to four distinct meanings (“never mentioned,” “explicitly cleared,” “unknown,” “not applicable”) flowing through two representations. Tony Hoare called null references his billion-dollar mistake; R doubled the budget. The only defense is an explicit, per-property presence policy.
Empty: an empty array, an empty object, and an absent key serialize differently and often mean different things ("layers": [] versus no layers key). Serializers need a stated omit-empty policy per field.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.8 Presence is a four-way decision, not a boolean
text:
4.8 Presence is a four-way decision, not a boolean
“Optional” conflates independent axes that a property model should separate:

Required at construction? May an object exist without a caller-supplied value? (Enforced by a quoted stop-default or constructor check.)
Nullable in the model? Is NULL a lawful stored value, typically meaning “omitted on the wire”? (Enforced by a NULL union member — and note the S7 subtlety that a union’s default prototype comes from its first member, so union order is load-bearing.)
Defaulted? Is there a domain-meaningful value when the caller is silent? (A real default is domain knowledge — alpha = 1 — not a placeholder.)
Omitted on serialization? Does an unset value vanish from the wire, or serialize as null/empty?

Every combination occurs in real specifications. Collapsing them into one optional = TRUE flag is how models end up unable to distinguish “user explicitly cleared this” from “user never touched this” — a distinction that matters enormously in patch/merge semantics and in round-tripping foreign documents.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.9 Literals, enums, and identity
text:
4.9 Literals, enums, and identity
A recurring puzzle when modeling specifications: a field whose value is fixed ("version": 8, "type": "geojson"). JSON Schema calls it const; TypeScript calls it a literal type. Three modeling options exist, and the choice is a genuine design decision, not a technicality:

Class identity. The field is not state at all; it is what the class is. Model it as a computed (getter-only) property or inject it at serialization. Two instances of the class can never differ on it, and it is not a constructor argument.
Stored with a default and a closed validator. The field is state that happens to have one lawful value today — the spec may add values, or round-tripping must preserve exactly what the wire said.
Constructor-normalized. Accept lenient input (8, 8L, even "8") at the boundary and store the canonical form.

The two questions that decide it: can two instances of this class ever differ on this value? (If no, it is identity, not state.) And must a round-trip preserve the user’s supplied value verbatim? (If yes, it must be stored.) Type discriminators in tagged unions (“this is a geojson source”) are almost always class identity — the class is the tag — while version fields are judgment calls that depend on whether one class will represent multiple spec versions.

title: 4  Types and Meaning: Semantic Types, Structure, and Type-Driven Design
section: 4.10 Refinements, for the statically minded
text:
4.10 Refinements, for the statically minded
If you come from typed languages, the property validator is best understood as a runtime refinement type: { x : numeric | 0 <= x && x <= 255 }. The class system checks the base type; the refinement predicate narrows it. This framing explains the layering rule in 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd — base type and refinement are checked in that order, and S7 formalizes it by validating class before calling the property validator — and it explains why refinements should be pure and cheap: they run at every construction and replacement, like a type check would.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
text:
5.1 The thesis, precisely
Alexis King’s 2019 essay “Parse, don’t validate” is often reduced to “check inputs early,” which misses its actual content. The distinction is about what happens to the knowledge a check produces.
A validator in her sense is a function like validateNonEmpty :: [a] -> (): it inspects, throws on failure, and returns nothing. The knowledge that the list was non-empty exists for one instant and is discarded; every later consumer either trusts blindly or checks again. A parser is parseNonEmpty :: [a] -> NonEmpty a: the same inspection, but the result is recorded in the type of the output. Downstream code that receives a NonEmpty a cannot even ask whether it is empty — the question has been settled, permanently, by construction.
Two named pathologies follow from doing it the other way. Shotgun parsing (a term from the language-theoretic security literature) is the anti-pattern of scattering input checks throughout processing code, interleaved with the processing itself — the program acts on input before fully deciding the input is well-formed, and rejection paths can fire after side effects have already happened. Boolean blindness (Robert Harper’s coinage) is the information loss of reducing a rich check to a TRUE/FALSE: the boolean remembers that something was true but not what or why, so the evidence must be reconstructed downstream — usually by checking again.
crumbs: 5  Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.2 The translation to a dynamic language
text:
5.2 The translation to a dynamic language
R has no compile-time types, so the slogan cannot mean “let the type checker carry proofs.” The translation is nonetheless faithful:
A parser is a boundary function that returns a domain object or fails loudly. Possession of the object is the proof.
Concretely, with S7: construction runs property class checks, property validators, and the class validator; every property replacement re-runs them. Therefore an S7 object of class Color that exists is evidence that its laws held at construction and after every legitimate modification since. A function receiving a Color needs no defensive re-checking of channel ranges — demanding the class (via dispatch or a property’s declared class) is the check. This is what “make illegal states unconstructable” buys: the object functions as a certificate.
Honesty requires noting the seams in a dynamic language. R will not stop someone from calling attr() surgery on the object’s internals, and S7 itself ships named escape hatches: S7::valid_eventually() suspends validation while a function runs and validates once at the end, while S7::valid_implicitly() suspends it and performs no final check — verified directly against S7 0.2.2: it will hand back an object that violates its own class validator. A getter can likewise return output that violates its declared class (getter output is not auto-validated). The guarantee is therefore conventional, and the precise phrasing matters: construction through the supported API is the runtime certificate, and it certifies only the laws actually encoded. Mutate through the front door — constructors, @<-, S7::set_props(), exported mutator functions — and the certificate holds. Package design reinforces the convention by exporting only the front door, and treats valid_implicitly() as what it is: an internal performance tool whose caller assumes the burden of proof.
crumbs: 5  Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.3 Constructors parse; validators verify
text:
5.3 Constructors parse; validators verify
The clean division of labor inside an S7 class:
Constructors (and boundary functions) normalize. They accept the messy input the outside world actually produces — a hex string or a channel array; a double 8 where an integer is meant; a bare scalar where a list is expected — and either produce canonical property values or abort with a user-facing error that names the argument (this is where cli::cli_abort() with rlang::caller_arg() context belongs). Coercion, canonicalization, and version gating are all parsing and all happen here, once.
Validators verify canonical values. By the time a validator runs, its input should already be in the one true representation; the validator’s job is to reject unlawful values, not to accommodate alternative shapes. A property validator that tolerates five input forms “for convenience” is a parser wearing a validator’s clothes — and since validators run on every construction and every property replacement, it re-runs its accommodation logic forever, on values that were already clean.
This is also Postel’s law put in its correct place: be liberal in what you accept at the boundary parser, and conservative everywhere else. The core of a well-built system is strict precisely because the boundary was generous.
crumbs: 5  Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.4 The checking ladder
text:
5.4 The checking ladder
Every check in a system has exactly one correct home. The rungs, from the outside world inward:
Rung 0 — external conformance validators. Full wire-format conformance — JSON Schema via AJV, an official specification validator, a database’s own constraint engine — belongs to the authority that owns the specification. Re-implementing an external spec’s full semantics inside property validators is expensive, drift-prone duplication. Published S7 packages are consistent on this: S7schema delegates YAML/JSON conformance to AJV; stacbuildr validates catalogs against the published STAC schemas; a style-document package should shell out to the official style validator for whole-document conformance. These run once, at the wire, not on every property write.
Rung 1 — boundary parsers. from_json(), read_as_markdown(), color_hex(): loose input in, domain objects out, cli-formatted errors with caller context on failure. All coercion lives here.
Rung 2 — property class. The declared class (possibly a union with NULL) is the base type check. S7 runs it before the property validator, so validators may assume the type.
Rung 3 — property validator. Local laws of one value: scalar-ness, length, range, set membership, pattern. Pure, cheap, no knowledge of any other property. Returns NULL or one message (without the property name — S7 prepends it, which is what makes property definitions reusable).
Rung 4 — setters. Normalization-on-write for meaning-preserving cleanup only. Used sparingly; a setter making semantic decisions is doing rung 1’s or rung 5’s job invisibly.
Rung 5 — class validator. Laws relating several properties of one object: ordering (start <= end), mutual exclusion, conditional requiredness. Receives self, returns NULL or a character vector of problems, refers to properties as @name. Must not repeat rungs 2–3.
Rung 6 — aggregate validator. Laws relating several objects in a containing structure: unique ids across a collection, references that must resolve, pairings between siblings. These belong to the lowest class that can see everything the law mentions — usually a root document object. This is Eric Evans’s aggregate from domain-driven design: the consistency boundary, whose root is the only thing outsiders hold and through which all modification flows. An invariant placed below its visibility horizon cannot be checked; placed above it, it runs too often and knows too much.
Rung 7 — operation preconditions. Some states are lawful to be in but unlawful to reach by a particular operation: adding a source whose id already exists, removing a source that layers still reference. These are workflow rules, not document laws — the document containing the source was always valid — so they live in the mutator functions (add_source(), remove_source()), erroring with cli::cli_abort() before any modification.
Rung 8 — internal assertions. Developer-facing checks for states the maintainer believes impossible, kept while refactoring, never part of the user contract.
Each rung assumes all rungs below it and duplicates none of them. The most common failure of validation architecture is not a missing check but the same law encoded on three rungs, which triples the maintenance surface and guarantees the encodings eventually disagree. When you find a law with two homes, delete one — or, more precisely, designate one home as authoritative. A deliberately retained cheap duplicate (a boundary check restating an inner law to produce a faster, better-localized error message) is a legitimate trade, provided it is documented as a duplicate and the authoritative rung is named. What the rule forbids is accidental multiplicity, where nobody knows which encoding governs.
crumbs: 5  Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.5 The cost model
text:
5.5 The cost model
Validators are not free, and their cost profile is part of the design. Property and class validators run at every construction and every property replacement — they are the hot path of the object system. Hence:

Validators must be pure (no I/O, no network, no reads of global state) and fast (no quadratic scans where avoidable).
Expensive conformance — full-document schema validation, cross-document consistency, anything touching disk — belongs on rungs 0–1, which run once per boundary crossing.
If an aggregate’s rung-6 validator becomes genuinely expensive (huge collections revalidated on every append), that is a signal to provide bulk constructors and batch mutators (build the whole collection, validate once) rather than to weaken the validator. S7 supplies the sanctioned mechanism: S7::valid_eventually(x, fun) suspends validation for the duration of fun and validates once at the end — a transaction in the literal sense, verified to pass through transient-invalid intermediate states and still reject an unlawful final state.

There is also a subtle transactionality consequence: because validation fires per replacement, invariants spanning multiple properties require atomic multi-property updates (S7::set_props()), or legitimate transitions will be rejected mid-flight. This was developed in 02-values-and-state.qmd.
crumbs: 5  Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.6 The time axis: as early as possible, as late as necessary
text:
5.6 The time axis: as early as possible, as late as necessary
The ladder places checks in space — which layer owns which law. Checks also have a placement in time, and the rule has two halves.
Shift left when the check needs nothing you don’t already have. The rtemis framework demonstrates both extremes of this. At the earliest possible moment: its property factories validate the declaration itself — a declared default outside its own declared bounds, or a double default on an integer property, “fails at factory time — i.e. at package load — rather than at first instantiation.” The author’s mistake surfaces before any user exists. At the last moment before expense: its setup_*() functions construct fully validated configuration objects before a training run that may fit thousands of models, so a typo in a hyperparameter costs milliseconds instead of hours. Both are the same principle: the value of a check is proportional to the cost of the work it gates, and it should run as far before that work as its inputs allow. A validated configuration object is itself a parse-don’t-validate move — the certificate is minted at setup time and trusted at run time.
Defer when the law mentions context that does not exist yet. Some constraints cannot be checked at construction because they relate the value to something external: rtemis’s data_bound properties declare that a hyperparameter is constrained by a training-data dimension (mtry bounded by the number of features; per-case weights matching the number of rows; feature selections that must be a subset of the column names). These are declared as data on the property and resolved in one pass, against the data, immediately before training begins — not smuggled into a validator that would have to guess, and not silently skipped. The general form: when a law spans the object and its eventual context, declare it at construction time and check it at the first moment the context is in hand, in one named place.
crumbs: 5  Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.7 Errors as values: the second channel
text:
5.7 Errors as values: the second channel
R’s condition system is a control-flow channel: an error unwinds the stack until something catches it. There is a second, complementary discipline in which failure travels through the data flow instead — the Result/Option family from Rust and the ML lineage — and the resultr package shows it is a natural fit for S7. Result is an abstract class existing purely for dispatch; Success and Failure are one-property variants; the combinator vocabulary (unwrap(), unwrap_or_else(), and_then(), expect()) is a set of generics with per-variant methods. The Failure method for and_then() just returns itself — which is the entire “railway-oriented programming” pattern in one line: once a pipeline is on the failure track, every subsequent step passes the failure through untouched, and the caller inspects the outcome once, at the end.
The architectural point is not “use Result everywhere”; conditions remain the right channel for bugs and contract violations (a validator rejecting an unlawful value should absolutely throw). Values are the right channel when failure is an expected outcome the caller will branch on as data — a batch of items where some fail and the survivors matter; a fallible lookup feeding a pipeline that should complete. What resultr gets exactly right is the conversion discipline: its wrap_in_result() generic converts conditions into values at one designed point (methods on class_error and class_warning wrap into Failure; everything else into Success; a Result passes through), inside a single rlang::try_fetch(). Two channels, one explicit adapter between them — never ad hoc tryCatch scattered through the middle of the system. It also enforces its certificates: the @value and @error properties use write-once setters that error on reassignment, making the outcome tamper-evident.
crumbs: 5  Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.8 Conditions: errors as a designed surface
text:
5.8 Conditions: errors as a designed surface
R’s condition system is unusually rich — conditions are classed, structured, signalable, catchable by class, and chainable — and a domain package should treat its error behavior as designed API, not incidental output. A workable stratification, aligned with the ladder:
User errors (rungs 1 and 7): the caller did something fixable. These deserve the full treatment — cli::cli_abort() with a message naming the argument (rlang::caller_arg()), attributed to the calling frame (rlang::caller_env()) so the error points at the user’s code rather than package internals, with a parent = chain when wrapping a lower-level failure. Message content should say what was expected, what arrived, and when possible what to do.
Invariant violations (rungs 3, 5, 6): terse declarative strings returned from validators — “must be between 0 and 255” — which S7 assembles into its own error, prefixing property names. These are not the place for cli markup or call-site attribution; they are law statements.
Warnings: recoverable degradation the caller should know about but need not stop for — a deprecated field mapped forward, a lossy normalization applied. Never use a warning where the result is unusable.
Progress and information: cli messaging in the shell, never in the core. A constructor that chatters is a constructor that cannot be used in a pipeline.
Classed conditions earn their keep the moment any caller needs to handle one failure differently from another: give programmatically distinguishable failures their own condition classes rather than making callers grep message text.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.9 Design by contract, and making it testable
text:
5.9 Design by contract, and making it testable
Bertrand Meyer’s design-by-contract vocabulary maps cleanly onto this architecture and is worth using in design discussions. Preconditions are rungs 1 and 7 — what must be true for the operation to proceed, the caller’s responsibility. Invariants are rungs 3, 5, 6 — what is always true of a lawful object, the class’s responsibility. Postconditions are the guarantees of the return value — largely carried by the returned type (parse-don’t-validate again: the strongest postcondition is “returns a Color”), plus documented promises like “the result’s getter outputs conform to their declared classes,” which S7 leaves on the author’s honor.
The contracts become testable in two complementary ways. Ordinary example tests exercise each rung: construction succeeds on lawful input, each unlawful input is rejected by the right rung with the right message, mutation through the front door revalidates, round-trips are identities. And law-based (property-based) testing generalizes them: state algebraic laws the domain must satisfy — serialization round-trips, order-insensitivity of collection construction, idempotence of normalization — and test them against generated inputs. The s7contract package packages exactly this for S7: explicit interface declarations (required generics), traits with registered implementations, optional runtime argument/return checking, and generative laws with shrinking. Whether or not one adopts the package, the mindset — an interface is a set of generics plus laws, and laws are executable — is the mature endpoint of validation thinking.

title: 5  Parse, Don’t Validate: Boundaries, the Checking Ladder, and Conditions
section: 5.10 The payoff, restated
text:
5.10 The payoff, restated
When the ladder is respected, a characteristic calm settles over the middle of the codebase. Core functions take domain objects and return domain objects; they contain no if (!is.character(x)) boilerplate, because rungs below them already settled it; their tests test logic, not plumbing. All the suspicion concentrates at the edges, where it belongs, in a small number of parsers with excellent error messages. The system’s trust structure becomes legible: you can point at any function and say exactly what it is entitled to assume and which rung guarantees it.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
text:
6.1 Algebraic data types: the half you already use and the half you underuse
The algebraic in “algebraic data types” refers to two constructions. Product types combine fields: a record with a name and an age and an email is the product of three sets. Every struct, every S7 class with properties, every data frame row is a product. Nobody needs convincing to use products.
Sum types (variants, tagged unions, discriminated unions) offer alternatives: a value is one of several possibilities, each possibly carrying different data. A network response is success-with-payload or failure-with-diagnostics. A message part is text or an image or a tool call. A map source is vector tiles or raster tiles or inline GeoJSON.
Sum types are the chronically underused half in mainstream OOP, and their absence has recognizable symptoms: boolean flag fields that change the meaning of other fields; clusters of mutually exclusive nullable fields (“exactly one of url and data must be set”); mode strings consulted by if/switch chains scattered across the codebase; validators full of conditional requiredness rules. Each of these is a sum type flattened into a product, with the discriminating structure pushed out of the representation and into runtime discipline. The type-driven move is to put the alternatives back into the representation — represent alternatives as alternatives.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
section: 6.2 Four encodings of sum types in S7
text:
6.2 Four encodings of sum types in S7
S7 has no native data Shape = Circle r | Square s, but it offers four encodings, each with a distinct profile.
1. Subclass family under an abstract parent. An abstract class anchors the concept; concrete subclasses are the variants:
Source <- S7::new_class("Source", abstract = TRUE)
VectorSource <- S7::new_class("VectorSource", parent = Source, properties = ...)
RasterSource <- S7::new_class("RasterSource", parent = Source, properties = ...)
This is the encoding of choice when variants differ in fields or in behavior: each subclass carries its own property schema, and generics dispatch per variant. It is nominal (each variant is a real class), open (new variants can be added, even by other packages), and integrates with property typing (prop = Source accepts any variant). Its cost is class-count and the absence of exhaustiveness checking, discussed below. The abstract parent exists for dispatch and shared schema; abstract = TRUE correctly prevents instantiating the concept-without-variant.
2. Anonymous union. S7::new_union(class_character, class_list) describes “either of these” for a property’s type, without creating any new class:
value = S7::new_property(S7::new_union(NULL, S7::class_character, S7::class_list))
Unions shine for alternatives of primitives in one slot — a value that is a literal or an expression; a field that is present or NULL. You cannot dispatch on “the union” (it is not a class), and there is a subtlety worth knowing: an unset property’s prototype derives from the union’s first member, so member order is load-bearing when defaults matter. Unions are structural glue, not domain concepts; when the alternative is a domain concept, prefer encoding 1.
3. Enum-valued property. When variants share all structure and differ only in a tag — a status that is pending, active, or closed, with no variant-specific fields — a constrained string property is the honest, cheapest encoding: a character scalar with a membership validator. The ecosystem has formalized this shape repeatedly: s7x ships an Enum class (value plus variants, validated), built exactly as an abstract parent with a class factory stamping out concrete enums. The moment one variant sprouts its own field, the enum has outgrown itself and wants encoding 1.
4. Discriminator plus conditional validator. One class holding a type tag and the union of all variants’ fields, with a class validator enforcing “if type is X, field Y must be set.” This is the flattened form the sum type was rescuing you from, and it is occasionally right anyway — when the wire format is genuinely one bag, variants are numerous and trivially different, and dispatch is never needed. Treat it as a deliberate denormalization, chosen consciously, not a default.
The selection logic compresses to three questions: Do variants differ in fields? Subclasses. Does behavior dispatch on the variant? Subclasses. Do variants differ only in the tag value? Enum property. Is it several primitive shapes in one slot? Union.

6.2.1 The canonical sum type, worked
The most famous sum type of all — Result = Success value | Failure error — exists as an S7 package, resultr, and it is worth reading as a reference implementation of encoding 1 at its purest. The abstract parent is documented as existing “for the purposes of dispatch”; each variant carries exactly one property; and the entire API is a generic vocabulary with per-variant methods, several of which are one-liners because the variant structure did all the work (and_then() on Failure returns x — that single method is short-circuiting error propagation). It also demonstrates two idioms worth having in the toolbox: write-once properties (a setter that errors if the slot is already non-NULL, approximating immutability enforcement for certificate-like fields) and multiple dispatch as argument typing (expect() registered on list(Success, class_character), so the message argument’s type participates in dispatch rather than being checked by hand). The deeper use of the pattern — errors traveling as values through data flow rather than as conditions through control flow — is developed in 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
section: 6.3 Living without exhaustiveness
text:
6.3 Living without exhaustiveness
ML-family languages check that every match handles every variant; S7 checks nothing of the sort, and this is the genuine loss in the translation. A new subclass silently satisfies no generics until methods are registered, and nothing at definition time lists what is missing. The working mitigations:

A loud default. Register a method on the abstract parent that fails with “no method for class X” — converting silent fallthrough into an immediate, named error at the first call.
Registry-driven tests. Keep the set of concrete variants enumerable (a list in the package, or discovered from the namespace) and write one test that iterates variants × required generics, asserting a method exists. This is exhaustiveness checking recovered as a unit test.
Sealed-hierarchy convention. Document which families are closed (only this package may add variants) versus open (extension expected). Closed families may rely on enumerating variants; open families must define the contract extenders implement — which is the interface question, below.
