title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
section: 6.4 Composition over inheritance — what the maxim actually claims
text:
6.4 Composition over inheritance — what the maxim actually claims
The Gang of Four’s “favor object composition over class inheritance” is a claim about implementation reuse: inheriting to acquire another class’s behavior couples you to its internals (the fragile base class problem — a parent’s private change breaks children that depended on incidental behavior), forces your concept into a single hierarchy axis, and multiplies subclasses combinatorially when independent dimensions vary (the ColoredBorderedScrollableWindow explosion).
Functional OOP softens the classic mechanism of the disease — an S7 parent contributes a property schema and a dispatch position, not a method table riddled with self-calls that subclasses override piecemeal — but the design rule survives fully intact:
Inherit for is-a and dispatch. Compose for has-a. Never inherit to reuse field names.

A VectorSource is a Source, participates in Source dispatch, and is substitutable wherever a Source is demanded: inheritance is honest.
A style has sources, layers, a light configuration: composition, always. Nesting objects as properties is the bread and butter of document modeling.
Two classes that coincidentally share three field names do not thereby have a parent. Extracting a parent from incidental structural overlap — schema cosplay — creates a nominal relationship that dispatch will eventually take seriously, wrongly.
Independent dimensions (a shape’s geometry versus its styling) belong in composed properties, not multiplied subclasses.

Healthy S7 hierarchies are consequently shallow: an abstract root naming the concept, one level of concrete variants, rarely a second level (and then only when an intermediate genuinely adds shared schema and a dispatch target, as with ellmer’s Turn → AssistantTurn → partial-turn refinements). Depth is a smell; width is normal.
Inheritance from a base type (parent = S7::class_character) is its own special case with its own honesty test: the object must genuinely be that primitive — a markdown document is text, an enum value is a string — such that treating it as the primitive is semantically sound, not merely convenient. When a concept has parts, wrapping structure into a subclassed primitive with a heroic validator fights the system; give it properties.
crumbs: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
section: 6.5 Encapsulation without access control
text:
6.5 Encapsulation without access control
R has no private. Every property of every S7 object is reachable with @, every internal function with :::. Encapsulation therefore cannot mean enforcement; it means a designed and documented public surface:

Exported constructors (possibly user-friendly wrappers over stricter internal ones), exported generics, exported mutators — the front door.
Unexported internals, free to change without deprecation.
Documentation that treats the exported surface as the contract.

This is Parnas’s information hiding in its original sense: modules hide design decisions likely to change, not secrets. The property layout of a class is such a decision; if churn is expected, exposing access through generics rather than documented @ paths preserves freedom to reorganize. The practical discipline from 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd applies: guarantees hold for clients who use the front door, and the package’s job is to make the front door the easiest path, not to bar the windows.
When compatibility demands a different surface — $ access, list-like behavior, an S3 class the ecosystem already handles — the answer is a facade: a thin S3 (or R6) exterior delegating to one internal S7 source of truth. One truth, two doors. Mirroring state across layers is how facades go wrong.
crumbs: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
section: 6.6 Dispatch as a design instrument
text:
6.6 Dispatch as a design instrument
Single dispatch is an open, extensible switch on class — the mechanism behind every polymorphic verb. Its design leverage comes from who owns which side: when you own the generic and others own classes, you have defined a plugin interface (ellmer owns chat-related generics; a third-party provider package adds a Provider subclass plus methods — the expression problem’s data axis, open). When you own classes and others own generics (print, format, S3 ecosystem verbs), method registration is your integration mechanism.
super(x, to = Parent) makes delegation up the hierarchy explicit — you name the parent whose behavior you want, rather than trusting an implicit resolution order (NextMethod()), which reads better and survives hierarchy refactors more loudly.
Multiple dispatch — generics dispatching on two or more arguments — is S7’s quiet superpower, inherited from the CLOS lineage and absent from mainstream message-passing OOP (which simulates it awkwardly via double dispatch/visitor patterns). It is rare, and where it applies nothing else is as clean: behavior that genuinely varies with two types at once. Published examples are instructive: sqlr defines render_sql <- new_generic("render_sql", c("x", "con")) — SQL generation varies by the object being rendered and the dialect of the connection, and each (type, dialect) pair is one small method rather than a matrix of conditionals. S7’s own convert(from, to) is dispatch on source and target. Interaction problems (combine, compare, coerce) are the recurring shape. The special classes class_any (match anything) and class_missing (match an absent argument) fill out the method tables without dummy classes.
crumbs: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
section: 6.7 Interfaces: sets of generics, plus laws
text:
6.7 Interfaces: sets of generics, plus laws
Functional OOP has no interface keyword because the concept is emergent: an interface is a set of generics a class supports, together with the laws those methods must satisfy. “Serializable” is: to_wire() and from_wire() exist, and from_wire(to_wire(x)) is x. The generics are checkable by dispatch; the law is checkable only by tests.
This implicitness is workable at small scale and frays at large scale, which is exactly the gap s7contract fills: explicit structural interfaces (named sets of required generics), traits (registered implementations with optional defaults and metadata), optional runtime checking of argument and return specifications, and — most valuably — generative laws: property-based tests with shrinking that verify the behavioral half of the contract, the half no dispatch table can see. The Go/Rust cultural import is deliberate and apt. Whether adopting the package or just the mindset, the design step it represents is the same: when you define an abstract class or an extension point, write down the laws an implementation must satisfy, as executable tests if at all possible.
Open families carry a lifecycle obligation that sealed ones escape: the extension contract itself evolves, and it can break extenders in a way class construction never reveals. Adding a required generic to an interface silently invalidates every third-party implementor — their classes still construct, their existing methods still dispatch, and the gap only surfaces when the new verb is called on their variant. The mitigations mirror wire formats, because an extension contract is a wire format between packages: introduce new verbs as optional with loud defaults on the abstract parent; publish a conformance test suite that extension packages run in their own checks (an executable statement of the current contract — s7contract’s interface checks are exactly this, packaged); and when a break is unavoidable, version the contract explicitly rather than letting extenders discover it at runtime.

title: 6  Composition and Dispatch: Sum Types, Hierarchy, Interfaces, and Indirection
section: 6.8 Indirection: every layer must pay rent
text:
6.8 Indirection: every layer must pay rent
David Wheeler’s aphorism — all problems in computer science can be solved by another level of indirection — comes with the standing corollary: except the problem of too many levels of indirection. Every abstraction in this document is indirection: the generic between caller and method, the semantic atom between meaning and primitive, the facade between surface and truth.
The test for whether a layer deserves to exist: does it absorb a real axis of variation? Rent-paying layers, concretely:

Generic → method absorbs variation of behavior across types that is actually observed (two-plus methods, or a genuine extension contract).
Semantic atom → primitive absorbs meaning: it prevents cross-wiring and centralizes a law that recurs.
Canonical spec → projections absorbs representation churn: one classification table generating a style expression and a legend and documentation means changes happen once.
Wire-name map → serializer absorbs naming churn between the domain model and evolving wire formats.

Rent-free layers, equally concretely: the wrapper class that adds no law and no dispatch; the interface with exactly one implementation and no second in sight; the factory abstracting a construction that occurs once; the parameter threaded through five functions “for flexibility” that no caller varies. The rule of three is the operational test — abstract on demonstrated recurrence, not anticipated recurrence — and deleting a rent-free layer is a design improvement, not a loss.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire
text:
7.1 The document-object-model pattern
A striking share of serious S7 usage models documents: a map style, a STAC catalog, a YAML configuration, a conversation transcript, a SQL statement, a typed program awaiting compilation. A document is a nested, typed, serializable value — declarative data with internal laws — and the recurring architecture for it deserves a name and an explicit anatomy:
crumbs: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire
text:
A class graph mirroring the document’s semantic structure. Composition edges (a style contains sources and layers; a catalog contains collections which contain items) become nested S7 properties. The graph is a tree of ownership.
Symbolic cross-references layered on the tree. Documents routinely encode relationships the tree cannot: a layer references a source by id; an item links to a collection by key. These are relational edges embedded in a hierarchical format — effectively foreign keys — and they generate the referential-integrity invariants (every reference resolves; ids are unique) that belong to an aggregate-root validator, per the ladder in 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd.
An aggregate root as the unit of consistency. Following Eric Evans: outsiders hold the root; all modification flows through it; its validator is the lowest point that sees every cross-object law. The root is also, naturally, the unit of serialization and of external validation.
Boundary constructors that lift native objects into the model. stacbuildr’s item_from_terra(), items_from_sf(), and lidR bridges are the pattern in its clearest form: users hold rasters and geometries, and the package parses those native objects into document nodes at the boundary, rather than asking users to hand-assemble metadata.
crumbs: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire
section: 7.2 Documents are programs; your package is a front-end
text:
7.2 Documents are programs; your package is a front-end
The deepest reframe available for this pattern: a declarative document is a program in a language you do not interpret. A map style is executed by a rendering engine; a STAC item is executed by search tooling; a SQL string by a database; a prompt-with-tools payload by an LLM provider. The R package producing such documents is therefore a compiler front-end: its job is to construct programs that are well-formed by construction, enforce the static semantics that are cheap and local (the ladder, rungs 1–6), and delegate full conformance to the engine’s own authority (rung 0).
This framing settles several recurring debates at once. Should the model validate everything the spec says? No — front-ends do not re-implement the runtime; the official validator owns full conformance. Should documents be built by string templating? No — compilers build structured representations and serialize once, because templates cannot enforce structure. Is hand-editing generated output acceptable? No — you do not patch a compiler’s output; you change the source and regenerate. And the imperative/declarative boundary becomes crisp: the document is declarative (what should exist); the pipeline that fetches inputs, builds it, writes it, uploads it is imperative shell around a functional core, per 02-values-and-state.qmd.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire
section: 7.3 Schema-driven development: postures toward an external schema
text:
7.3 Schema-driven development: postures toward an external schema
Most documents come with a schema — JSON Schema, a TypeScript definition file, an OpenAPI component set, protobuf. Three postures toward consuming one recur, and mature designs usually combine the first two; a fourth relationship, pointing the opposite direction, appears when the model itself is the source of truth.
Schema as boundary contract. Validate wire input and output against the schema, mechanically, using the schema ecosystem’s own tooling. S7schema is this posture productized: YAML configuration in, AJV validation against JSON Schema via V8, and only then S7/list objects out for downstream typed extension. stacbuildr validates against the published STAC schemas. The posture is cheap, authoritative, and evolution-friendly (schema versions are explicit). Keep it wherever tooling exists.
Schema as design input. Read the schema as evidence about the domain: census which property shapes recur (how many enum fields, how many bounded numbers, how many string-or-expression slots), which fields are required, where the sum types hide (oneOf with a discriminator), what is genuinely extensible (additionalProperties). Then design the semantic layer — atoms, composites, variant families — informed by the census but organized around meaning. This is data-driven design in the first sense of 03-types-and-meaning.qmd, and it is where design quality is actually determined.
Schema as codegen source. Mechanically emit one class per schema object. This is the tempting posture and almost always the wrong one, for a reason worth stating carefully: schemas encode structure, not semantics. A TypeScript interface file will happily contain fifteen interfaces that are structurally distinct but semantically one concept (a color, expressed fifteen ways), and zero indication of which nesting is a real domain object versus a serialization artifact. A 1:1 mirror faithfully imports the structure while discarding the one thing a domain model adds — meaning — and saddles you with a class count that tracks the schema’s quirks forever. What does mechanize well is the regular substrate: enum value tables, wire-name maps, requiredness matrices, version constants. Generate tables, not class graphs; hand-design the classes from the census.
One legitimate exception deserves its own name so it stops being argued case by case: the generated transport model. When faithful transport is itself the requirement — an API surface too large and too churn-prone to hand-model, consumed mostly by code generators downstream — mechanically generated wire types are appropriate, provided they are labeled as transport and kept behind boundary parsers that lift them into the hand-designed domain layer (domain-driven design calls this arrangement an anti-corruption layer). The two models coexist: generated types absorb the schema’s churn; semantic types carry the meaning. The anti-pattern was never generation itself — it is mistaking the generated transport model for the domain model, which is what “schema cosplay” names.
The reverse arrow: schema as projection. The three postures above concern consuming an external schema. There is a fourth relationship, pointing the other way: when the domain model is the source of truth, the schema is one of its outputs. This only becomes possible under a specific precondition — constraints must be stored as data, not encoded as closures. A validator function can enforce a range but cannot be asked what the range is; a spec object carrying minimum and maximum fields can do both. rtemis is the fully developed exhibit: its property factories attach a PropertySpec object recording type, bounds, enum, nullability, container shape, and a dozen further axes as plain data, and from that one declaration the package mechanically derives the R validator, the default, a JSON Schema (via S7_to_JSONSchema()), and a TUI configuration form. sqlr is the same arrow in SQL: the schema value renders to per-dialect DDL, compares structurally, and diffs — projections a bag of CREATE TABLE strings could never support. The payoff in both cases is the single-source-of-truth guarantee: the validator and the published schema cannot disagree, because both are projections of one datum. When you find yourself writing a validator and separately documenting its rule, that is the signal this arrow wants to exist.
A compact translation guide from external constructs to S7 mechanisms:







External construct
S7 mechanism




const / literal type
class identity: computed property or serializer-injected constant


enum, closed
validated character property (or a formalized enum class)


enum, extensible
validated character property plus a parse-boundary version gate


oneOf with discriminator
abstract parent + subclass family; the tag is class identity


oneOf of primitives
S7::new_union() on the property


allOf / interface extension
composition first; a parent class only if is-a is honest


additionalProperties
a pass-through bag property with key discipline only


nullable / optional
NULL union member + explicit presence policy (four axes)


nested object
composed S7 class


array of typed objects
list property with a membership validator

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire
section: 7.4 Serialization: one pair of functions knows the wire
text:
7.4 Serialization: one pair of functions knows the wire
Serialization discipline compresses to a single rule: exactly one place in the package knows what the wire looks like — a to_wire() projection and a from_wire() parser, usually generic-dispatched over the class graph.
The projection owns: wire-name mapping (source_layer → "source-layer"), the omit-empty policy per field (absent key versus null versus [], per the presence axes of 03-types-and-meaning.qmd), injection of identity constants (version numbers, type tags), and recursive descent through composed objects. The parser owns: version gating, coercion into canonical representations, the unknown-key policy, and construction through the front door so every law is checked on entry.
Round-tripping is a law, not an aspiration: from_wire(to_wire(x)) should equal x, and to_wire(from_wire(doc)) should preserve every field you claim to preserve. State the law, test it against gold files, and where the round trip is deliberately lossy (normalization collapses equivalent forms), document the quotient explicitly. This is the most valuable single test family a document package can have, because it exercises the entire class graph, both boundary functions, and the presence policy at once.
Stating the law precisely requires naming the equivalence relation, because “equals” hides four different contracts: representational identity (identical(), byte-for-byte); canonical equality (equal after normalization to the one stored form); semantic equivalence (equal ignoring non-meaningful variation — ordering, auto-generated names, whitespace); and wire equivalence (equal once omitted fields and defaults are resolved). Each round-trip promise should say which relation it uses, and for most document systems the honest law is canonical equality, not identity. sqlr models the discipline: its sqlr_equal() implements semantic equivalence — constraints matched on what they constrain rather than their order or auto-generated names — and its README says so explicitly, which is what makes a hand-written schema comparable to a reflected one.
Two packages show how far the round-trip law scales as an organizing idea. sqlr’s counterpart to from_wire() is sqlr_reflect(), which reads a live database’s catalog back into the same schema representation the renderer consumes; the README calls the resulting equality “the package’s own test oracle,” and makes it meaningful by defining equality structurally — constraints matched on what they constrain rather than on order or auto-generated names, so a hand-written schema compares equal to a reflected one. typedjson goes further: the round trip is not a test of the product, it is the product — faithful, human-readable JSON for R values, achieved by annotating only what JSON cannot natively express (integer versus double, typed missing values, non-finite numbers, attributes, objects from the S3, S4, and S7 systems). Its design rule — keep ordinary JSON for ordinary values and add the minimum machinery that makes the identity hold — is presence policy elevated to a format’s founding principle.
One structural decision deserves early attention: open versus closed nodes. Foreign documents may carry extensions you do not model. A closed node rejects unknown keys (maximal law enforcement, brittle against spec evolution); an open node carries them through in a pass-through bag (round-trip fidelity for foreign content, weaker guarantees). Real formats need both, chosen per node — strict where you claim semantics, permissive where the format is deliberately extensible (metadata blocks, vendor extensions). What does not work is deciding by accident.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire
section: 7.5 Expression languages and the AST escalation ladder
text:
7.5 Expression languages and the AST escalation ladder
Documents frequently embed a second, smaller language: filter and styling expressions inside map styles, query fragments, template strings, tool-call schemas. The design question — how much structure to give the embedded language — has a clean escalation ladder, and the discipline is to climb only when the next rung’s analysis is actually needed.
Rung 1: opaque passthrough. The expression is a list (or string) the model stores and emits verbatim; the engine’s validator is its only judge. Zero modeling cost, zero analysis capability. This is the correct default, and treating it as the default is what prevents the most seductive over-engineering in document modeling: rebuilding the engine’s expression type system in validators, forever, badly.
Rung 2: constructor combinators. Functions that build correct expressions — expr_match(field, cases), expr_interpolate(...) — giving ergonomics, spelling safety, and partial static checking at construction time, while the representation stays the wire’s own (lists). This is a shallow embedding of the foreign language: the combinators are the DSL, and they compile immediately to the target form. Most packages should stop here; it captures the bulk of the value (humans stop hand-writing nested lists) at a fraction of the cost.
Rung 3: a typed AST. Node classes for the expression language, generic passes over them — type checking, optimization, translation to multiple targets. This is a deep embedding: the program is data (S7 objects), and interpretation is a separate, swappable step. It is exactly what quickr is — R functions with declare(type()) annotations parsed into a typed S7 intermediate representation (typed nodes for subroutines, operations, analyses), passes over that IR, and Fortran emission at the back —, and what dbplyr does for SQL in S3 terms. The rung is justified when analysis or multi-target translation is the product; it is pure cost when the only consumer re-serializes to the single original wire format.
The general lesson generalizes past expressions: representation should be as deep as your analysis, and no deeper.

title: 7  Documents, Schemas, and Languages: Object Models at the Wire
section: 7.6 DSLs and metaprogramming: R’s home turf, with guardrails
text:
7.6 DSLs and metaprogramming: R’s home turf, with guardrails
R is unusually good at embedded DSLs — quotation (quote(), bquote()), first-class environments, lazy evaluation, and rlang’s quasiquotation make building little languages almost frictionless, which is precisely why restraint is a design skill. Two patterns earn their keep in object-system work:
Checks as data. Validator logic represented as composable quoted expressions, assembled by a single function-builder into ordinary, inspectable validator functions (rlang::new_function() over a spliced body). This is a micro deep-embedding of a checking language, and it solves a real problem — validator factories that call validator factories accumulate argument-forwarding bugs; flat quoted checks compose without nesting. The guardrails: generated functions must be inspectable (printing the body shows exactly the checks, in order), directly testable (call the generated validator in tests, not just the factory), and built by splicing quoted expressions — never by eval(parse(paste0(...))), which abandons hygiene, tooling, and safety at once.
Classes as data. Because S7 classes are first-class values (01-object-systems.qmd), factories that return classes are ordinary code: an enum-class factory stamping variants from a character vector (the s7x pattern), a family generator producing parallel node classes from a table. The same guardrails apply, plus one more: generate structural regularity only. The moment generated classes need per-class special cases, the generator has become an obfuscation layer over what should be ordinary, readable class definitions.
Both patterns assume the quoted material originates inside the package. The moment expressions, extension bags, or class metadata arrive from outside — a file, a wire, a user — the concern changes from hygiene to security, and the rules harden: never evaluate untrusted text or quoted structures; treat deserialization as parsing (rung 1 of the checking ladder), never as object restoration by fiat; keep pass-through extension bags inert data until something explicitly chooses to interpret them; and bound recursion depth and payload size before walking untrusted nested structures, because a parser that recurses on hostile input is a denial of service waiting for its input.
The boundary that keeps metaprogramming honest is the one this whole document has been drawing: mechanize the regular, hand-write the meaningful. Wire-name tables, enum catalogs, repetitive property shapes — generate. Domain concepts, invariants, the verb vocabulary — write, by hand, where readers will look for them.

text:
8.1 Cluster A — Values, state, and architecture
Each package below was verified against its current documentation or source (September 2026). The interest is not in their domains but in the design moves they demonstrate — each is the clearest available exhibit for at least one pattern from the preceding documents. The guide is organized into five thematic clusters, with cross-cutting observations at the end.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: What Real S7 Packages Teach
text:
8.1.1 ellmer — the hybrid architecture, and dispatch as a plugin system
ellmer (tidyverse; LLM chat from R) is the reference example for mixing object systems by semantics rather than ideology. The Chat object is R6, and the documentation is explicit about why: a conversation is mutable state with identity — you send messages to it, it accumulates turns, it runs the tool-invocation loop — and value semantics would force callers to reassign after every exchange. Branching a conversation requires an explicit $clone(), exactly the ceremony value semantics would have made free, and ellmer accepts that trade consciously.
Everything flowing through the Chat is S7 values: Turn (with UserTurn, SystemTurn, AssistantTurn subclasses — a sum type as a subclass family, where the assistant variant carries extra fields like tokens, cost, and finish reason), Content objects inside turns (text, images, tool requests, tool results — another variant family), Model (a small immutable configuration value), and Provider. Records of fact are values; the ongoing process is a reference.
The Provider hierarchy doubles as the package’s plugin system: the README lists ten official and nine community providers, and supporting a new LLM service means subclassing Provider and registering methods on the existing generic vocabulary for request building and response parsing. The data axis of the expression problem, held open on purpose — community providers extend ellmer without touching its core.


8.1.2 ragnar — honest base-type inheritance and the enriched table
ragnar (tidyverse; retrieval-augmented generation) contributes two small, perfect exhibits.
MarkdownDocument is an S7 class inheriting from character: a document is a length-one markdown string, with an @origin property riding along. The inheritance passes the honesty test of 05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd — treating the object as text is semantically sound, not merely convenient. Its constructor is a boundary parser in miniature: it normalizes (collapses lines, enforces UTF-8) so that, quoting the docs, “downstream code can rely on a consistent format” — parse-don’t-validate stated as user documentation.
MarkdownDocumentChunks inherits from tibble: chunk data is genuinely tabular (start, end, context columns; users will filter and mutate it), so it should be a data frame — but it carries the source document as a @document property, keeping the provenance attached to the value rather than in a parallel variable the user must not lose. An enriched table: structural behavior from the base class, domain identity and payload from S7.


8.1.3 tooey — the Elm architecture as a whole-program design
tooey (devOpifex) is a terminal UI framework built on the Model–View–Update architecture (The Elm Architecture): an application is three pure functions — init(model) producing initial commands, update(model, msg) mapping a state and a message to a new state plus commands, and view(model, buf) rendering state into a screen buffer — while a runtime loop owns the terminal, the clock, and input events, feeding them in as messages (is_key, is_tick) and executing returned commands (cmd_tick, cmd_quit).
This is the functional core / imperative shell of 02-values-and-state.qmd in its most disciplined published form: all state transitions are pure data-to-data functions, all effects are values (commands) interpreted by the shell, and the framework — not convention — enforces the boundary. Even in a domain as imperative-seeming as a live terminal UI, mutation is confined to a runtime the application author never touches. It is also a working answer to “where do messages and events fit in a value-oriented design”: as plain data dispatched over, exactly like any other variant family.

section: 8.2 Cluster B — Documents, schemas, and serialization
text:
8.2 Cluster B — Documents, schemas, and serialization

8.2.1 stacbuildr — the document-object-model pattern, complete
stacbuildr (STAC geospatial catalogs) is the fullest single exhibit of 06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd: STAC 1.1.0 Catalogs, Collections, and Items as an S7 class graph, serialized to STAC JSON, validated against the published JSON schemas (rung 0 delegated to the specification’s own authority), with extensions (electro-optical, raster, projection, and more) layered onto the core following the spec’s own shared bands model.
Two moves stand out beyond the basics. First, the boundary-constructor family: item_from_terra(), item_from_sf(), item_from_lidr() lift native geospatial objects — rasters, geometries, point clouds users already hold — into document nodes, extracting extents, projections, and band metadata at the boundary. Second, the document as data: a Collection supports length(), [[, as.data.frame() (one row per item, properties as columns, list-columns for structured values), and sf::st_as_sf() — the object graph projects into the tabular and spatial idioms R users already know, rather than forcing graph navigation. Its write_stac() also encodes the STAC best-practices catalog layouts (self-contained, relative, absolute) as an explicit enum that maps one-to-one onto PySTAC’s CatalogType — cross-ecosystem vocabulary alignment as API design.


8.2.2 S7schema — schema as boundary contract, productized
S7schema (Novo Nordisk; CRAN) is the schema-as-boundary-contract posture as a reusable framework: YAML configuration files validated against JSON Schema definitions using AJV (via V8), with the resulting configuration objects inheriting from both S7 classes and base lists — full conformance checking delegated to the schema ecosystem’s standard tooling, R-side typing layered on for downstream extension through custom classes and methods. Notably it does not re-derive the schema’s rules as property validators — the two layers check different things.


8.2.3 rapid — an external specification as a strict domain object
rapid (api2r) converts OpenAPI descriptions into R objects of a new S7 class that, in its own words, “enforces a strict, opinionated schema.” The design posture is instructive: rather than wrapping the OpenAPI JSON loosely, it parses the specification into a validated domain object intended as the substrate for downstream code generation (the beekeeper and mockplumber packages). An API description is exactly the kind of declarative document 06 describes, and rapid is the front-end that makes it lawful before generators consume it — parse once at the boundary, generate from the certified object.


8.2.4 sqlr and its dialects — schema as the middle term, round-trip as oracle
nbenn/sqlr has matured into one of the most architecturally articulate S7 packages anywhere, and its README states its thesis in one sentence: what R lacked was “a representation of a schema that is neither a string nor a connection, which you can build, render, reflect and compare.” That middle term — the schema as a first-class value between the DDL text and the live database — is the document-object-model argument made for SQL.
Four design moves reward study. Dialects are objects, not connections: rendering (sqlr_render(schema, sqlite())) needs no server, no driver, and the core package renders nothing on its own — dialect packages (sqlr.postgres, sqlr.sqlite) supply the spellings via multiple dispatch (render_sql(x, con) dispatching on object and dialect at once). There is deliberately no generic fallback: nothing renders “ANSI SQL,” because no engine implements it faithfully and “an untestable default would quietly accumulate behaviour no database had ever accepted” — an unregistered dialect is an error rather than a guess. Reflection closes the loop: sqlr_reflect(con) reads a live database’s catalog back into the same representation sqlr_render() consumes, and the round trip (sqlr_equal(schema, sqlr_reflect(con))) is, in the package’s own words, “the package’s own test oracle.” Equality is structural and semantic: constraints and indexes are matched on what they constrain, not their order or auto-generated names, so a hand-written schema compares equal to a reflected one — and sqlr_diff() reports meaningful differences, the explicit groundwork for a future migration generator. Rendering even performs real compilation work: tables emit in dependency order and cycle-closing foreign keys are lifted into trailing ALTER TABLE statements.


8.2.5 typedjson — round-trip fidelity as the entire product
typedjson (same author) makes the round-trip law of 06 into a package: it “writes an R value as JSON a human can read, and reads it back unchanged.” Its README diagnoses the existing landscape precisely — jsonlite is readable but lossy (doubles return as integers, all-NA vectors lose their type, empty typed vectors collapse to list()), serializeJSON is faithful but unreadable — and stakes out the missing quadrant: ordinary JSON for ordinary values, with annotations only for what JSON cannot express (integer versus double, typed missing values, non-finite doubles, attributes, language objects, and S3/S4/S7 objects). That principle — annotate the minimum needed to make the round trip an identity — is the presence-policy and wire-universe discussion of 03-types-and-meaning.qmd turned into a serialization format.


8.2.6 structr — the contrast case: a compiled schema, not an object system
structr (ixpantia) is deliberately not S7 — it is Rust (serde, simd_json) behind an R schema DSL (s_map(), s_integer(), s_optional(), build_structure()) — and it earns its place here as the boundary of the boundary. structr compiles a schema once and then parses and serializes against it, strictly: type mismatches, missing fields, and unexpected nulls are errors. It is rungs 0–1 of the checking ladder as a standalone, high-performance tool, with no domain objects at all — the output is plain R lists that are known to conform. The lesson is about division of labor: when the need is pure wire conformance at speed, a compiled schema validator beats an object system, and an S7 domain layer is what you build on top of such a boundary when invariants, identity, and dispatch are needed beyond the parse. Its “all fields required unless s_optional()” default is also the right polarity for presence policy — opt into looseness, never out of it.

section: 8.3 Cluster C — Errors, contracts, and introspection
text:
8.3 Cluster C — Errors, contracts, and introspection

8.3.1 resultr — errors as values, the Result/Option sum type
resultr implements Rust’s Result/Option vocabulary in S7, and its Result.R is a compact tour of the sum-type playbook: an abstract Result parent “used for the purposes of dispatch,” Success and Failure subclasses each carrying one property, and the full monadic combinator set as generics — unwrap(), unwrap_or_default(), unwrap_or_else(), and_then(), inspect(), expect() — with per-variant methods (the Failure method for and_then simply returns itself, which is railway-oriented short-circuiting).
Three details are worth stealing. First, the boundary between conditions and values is a generic: wrap_in_result() has methods for class_any (wrap in Success), class_error and class_warning (wrap in Failure), and Result itself (pass through) — so R’s condition system is converted into value-level errors at exactly one point, inside and_then()’s rlang::try_fetch(). Second, write-once properties: both @value and @error use a setter that errors if the slot is already set — a poor man’s immutability enforcement, making the certificate tamper-evident. Third, expect() dispatches on list(Success, class_character) — multiple dispatch pressed into service for argument typing. The broader lesson feeds 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd: R has two error channels, conditions (control flow) and values (data flow), and a design should choose per boundary which one crosses it.


8.3.2 s7contract — interfaces, traits, and executable laws
s7contract (CRAN) imports the Go-interface/Rust-trait worldview onto S7 dispatch, and its README now shows the full progression. Structural interfaces are named sets of required generics, checked by method availability (implements(Circle, Shape)), with missing_requirements() reporting exactly which verb is absent — Go’s implicit satisfaction, made queryable. Traits require explicit impl_trait() registration and support default methods and associated constants — Rust’s explicit opt-in. Progressive runtime checks let an interface requirement carry argument and return specifications, enforced in contract-scoped evaluation (with(Interface, expr)), so a method that returns the wrong type fails at the call with a typed message. Generative laws combine named generators, shrinking, and tinytest expectations (expect_law()), testing the behavioral half of the contract that no dispatch table can see. Its stated limits are as instructive as its features: all checks are runtime, and passing generated cases proves nothing universally — honest about what a dynamic language can and cannot recover of Rust’s compile-time story.


8.3.3 datarr (reflect) — the metaobject payoff of classes-as-values
datarr (package name reflect) builds runtime reflection for base R and S7: immutable descriptor objects for properties, methods, and callables, with explicit capability predicates. Its s7.R shows what S7’s classes-as-first-class-values design makes possible in ordinary R code: reflect_properties() walks class@properties and the constructor’s formals to report each property’s declared type, default presence, requiredness (a formal equal to the empty symbol), validator presence, and whether it is inherited (tracing the declaring class up the parent chain); reflect_methods() enumerates a generic’s method table and can attach S7’s own method_explain() dispatch trace; reflect_callable() distinguishes generics, methods, and closures with their signatures. The descriptors are themselves S7 objects — reflection modeled in the system being reflected.
Two further touches: reflect_validate() wraps S7::validate() with a chained, classed condition (the error-design discipline of 04 applied to the metalevel), and reflect_check_project() audits a package against declared conventions (export naming policy, dependency policy, lifecycle documentation) — conventions turned into executable checks, which is the same move as s7contract’s laws applied to project structure instead of object behavior.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: What Real S7 Packages Teach
section: 8.4 Cluster D — Systems built on S7 at scale
text:
8.4 Cluster D — Systems built on S7 at scale

8.4.1 rtemis — constraints as data, one declaration to rule four artifacts
rtemis (machine learning framework, 150+ stars) rewrote its entire supervised/unsupervised backend from R6 and S3 onto S7, and its 010_Props.R is the most sophisticated property foundation yet published. The core idea: every prop_* factory attaches a PropertySpec — a nested S7 object in which the property’s type, bounds, enum, default, nullability, and roughly twenty further axes are stored as data rather than closures. Because the constraints are data, one declaration mechanically produces four artifacts: the R validator, the default, a JSON Schema (via S7_to_JSONSchema()), and downstream a TUI configuration form. This is the “one canonical artifact, many projections” principle executed at the level of individual properties, and it is the reverse arrow of schema-driven development: the model generates the schema.
The spec’s axes are a checklist of presence-and-arity distinctions most designs never separate: container (none / array / map / matrix / table / struct / factor, each with a documented rationale — a factor serializes as {levels, codes} because a label array would lose level order and empty levels); broadcast (a scalar stands for the whole container) kept mutually exclusive with tunable (an array alongside a value is a search space, one nesting level above the value’s own type — the comment warns “a reader must never infer one from the other’s shape”); tune_on_null versus default_on_null (two different meanings of NULL, declared rather than guessed); constant (class identity) versus fixed-but-settable; applies_when (conditional applicability among sibling properties, encoded as data and checked centrally); and data_bound — validity constraints tied to training-data dimensions (n_features, n_cases, class names) that cannot be checked at construction and are instead resolved in one pass against the data before any training begins.
Around this foundation sit two more discipline exhibits. Factory-time validation: a PropertySpec’s validator checks that the declared default conforms to its own spec, so a bad declaration “fails at factory time — i.e. at package load — rather than at first instantiation.” Eager configuration validation: the user-facing setup_*() functions (setup_LightGBM(), setup_GridSearch()) construct validated configuration values before a run that may train thousands of models, so user error surfaces in milliseconds, not hours. There is even an authorship-policy annotation (agent_writable) deliberately excluded from published schemas because who may set a property can change while what the property is cannot — a crisp example of keeping volatile policy out of stable contracts.


8.4.2 quickr — S7 as a compiler’s intermediate representation
quickr (Tomasz Kalinowski; CRAN) compiles R functions to Fortran. Users annotate functions with an in-language type DSL — declare(type(x = double(NA))), a runtime no-op the compiler reads, expressing element modes, shapes, and size relationships between arguments (double(n) twice means “same length”) — and quick() lowers the R code through a typed intermediate representation to generated Fortran compiled via R CMD SHLIB. That IR is S7: typed values (e.g. a FortranSubroutine consumed as fsub@name, fsub@closure) flow between compiler stages. This is rung 3 of the AST escalation ladder, justified because analysis and translation are the product. The broader pattern — R syntax as source language, S7 objects as typed IR, a foreign language as target — recurs wherever multi-target analysis appears.


8.4.3 optimizers7 and parameters7 — extracting the private re-implementations
The statmodels7 family (optimizers7, parameters7, with distributions7, linkfunctions7, basis7 as siblings) is built on one sharp observation, stated in both READMEs: almost every modeling package privately re-implements the same mathematics — optimizers as while (!converged) loops with “a tolerance compared against whatever quantity the author had to hand,” constrained parameters as bespoke parametrizations (nlme’s pdMat, lme4’s theta, every mixture package’s softmax) — “none exposing a derivative, none reusable from outside.”
The response is semantic atoms at the level of mathematical behavior: an optimizer is an S7 object carrying its algorithm and settings, written once against one objective interface; a stopping rule is a separate, composable object — the observation that “the stopping rule, which decides what the whole procedure means by finished, is usually a number buried three levels down” is an indirection-rent argument of unusual clarity. A constrained parameter is “a fixed mathematical object: a map from an unconstrained vector onto the set where the parameter lives … with its inverse, its derivatives, and the quantities a likelihood asks of the value” — evaluated, inverted, differentiated to fourth order, as an object. Both packages are also deliberately narrow (“an optimizer here minimizes the function it is given, with no notion of an observation”) — boundary discipline about which layer is allowed to know what.

section: 8.5 Cluster E — Foundations and utilities
text:
8.5 Cluster E — Foundations and utilities

8.5.1 s7x and the R-ArcGIS stack — convergent evolution of the foundation layer
s7x (Josiah Parry) is a utility layer over S7 providing an extensible Enum class (value + variants, validated, castable to character), scalar properties, range properties, and property unions and intersections. The R-ArcGIS packages (arcgisutils, arcgisviz) consume it at scale to model a very large TypeScript-shaped API surface. Together with rtemis’s PropertySpec factories and the private property-factory layers appearing in document-modeling codebases, this is now a three-way independent convergence on the same helper stratum — enum formalization, scalar/bounded factories, presence-aware wrappers — which is strong evidence about which foundation abstractions are genuinely load-bearing.


8.5.2 objectstore — interface-first design, embryonic
objectstore (Hugo Gruson) is an “Object Store Interface in R with S7” at a very early stage (a handful of commits). Its interest is the shape of the bet: defining the abstract interface to object storage as the package’s product, with backends to dispatch beneath it — the generic-vocabulary-as-plugin-contract pattern (ellmer’s Providers, sqlr’s dialects) applied to storage. One to watch rather than to study yet.


8.5.3 provider — the adjacent case
provider (healthcare provider APIs) is included for completeness as a data-domain API client in this orbit; its published surface is a tidyverse-style httr2 client rather than an S7 architecture. It illustrates the before state of the patterns in this guide — a domain of record types (providers, enrollments, claims) currently represented as tibbles, which is entirely reasonable, and exactly the kind of surface where semantic atoms and typed records would be the next step if invariants started to matter.

title: 8  Ecosystem Field Guide: What Real S7 Packages Teach
section: 8.6 Cross-cutting observations
text:
8.6 Cross-cutting observations
Reading the ecosystem as a whole rather than package by package:
Hybrids are the norm, not the exception. ellmer (R6 + S7), ragnar (S7 + tibble), S7schema (S7 + list + V8/AJV), sqlr (S7 generics + S4 DBI connections), structr (Rust boundary + plain R values), tooey (pure functional core + runtime shell). Mature designs choose per-object semantics and let the compatibility layer do its job.
Constraints-as-data keeps winning. rtemis stores property constraints in a spec object and generates validators, schemas, and forms from it; sqlr stores a schema as a value and generates DDL, comparisons, and diffs from it; rapid parses OpenAPI into a strict object that generators consume; structr compiles a schema once and parses against it. The common shape: represent the contract as inspectable data, derive every enforcement and projection mechanically, and never encode the same fact twice.
Round-trip as oracle recurs independently. sqlr’s render/reflect equality is “the package’s own test oracle”; typedjson’s entire product is the identity round trip; stacbuildr writes and reads catalogs through the same representation. When a package models a wire format, the round-trip law is the highest-value test it can own.
Errors have two channels, and good designs choose deliberately. Conditions (rlang/cli, chained, classed — datarr’s reflect_validate) for control-flow errors; values (resultr’s Result, converted from conditions at exactly one boundary) for data-flow errors. The anti-pattern is mixing them ad hoc.
Base-type inheritance appears exactly where it is honest. A markdown document is text (ragnar); an enum value is a string (s7x). Nobody publishes a subclassed primitive stuffed with structure.
Multiple dispatch is rare and decisive. sqlr’s render_sql(x, con) (object × dialect), resultr’s expect(Success, class_character), S7’s own convert(from, to). Everywhere it appears, the alternative was a conditionals matrix.
Rung 0 is always delegated. stacbuildr to the STAC schemas, S7schema to AJV, sqlr to the actual database engines (refusing even to pretend a generic dialect exists), structr to a compiled Rust validator. None re-implements an external specification internally.
The document-object-model shape recurs across unrelated domains. Catalogs, configurations, conversations, styles, SQL schemas, API descriptions, typed IRs, even terminal screens (tooey’s buffer): nested values, aggregate roots, boundary parsers, projection serializers. The domain changes; the anatomy does not.

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
text:
9.1 Principles
This document compresses the whole research folder into what you would actually use in a design session: nineteen principles stated as prose, five decision guides stated as questions, and a catalog of named anti-patterns with their failure narratives. Nothing here is new; everything is justified in the earlier documents.
A register note before the principles: everything in this document is doctrine — deliberately imperative defaults distilled from documented S7 behavior and observed ecosystem practice, but laws of neither. The imperative mood is a choice: a crisp default you can overrule for stated reasons is more useful in a design session than a hedge you can ignore. “Always” and “never” here mean “strong default,” and when a principle collides with a real constraint, the earlier documents carry the reasoning needed to make the trade explicitly.
1. Model meaning before structure. Begin with the domain’s semantic atoms — the indivisible meanings and their laws — and only then compose the document structures that arrange them. Structure is the volatile part; meaning is the stable contract. Systems (and dialects of a domain) that share semantics can differ in structure and still interoperate; systems that share only structure are totally coupled.
2. Let construction be the proof. Arrange the system so that no unlawful object of a class can exist: boundary functions parse loose input into objects or fail loudly, validators run on construction and every replacement, and possession of the object certifies its laws. Downstream code demands classes instead of re-checking contents.
3. Constructors normalize; validators verify; boundaries translate. Coercion, canonicalization, and version gating happen once, at the boundary. Validators judge canonical values only, and stay pure and cheap because they run on every property write. A validator accommodating multiple input shapes is a parser in the wrong place, running forever.
4. Every invariant has one authoritative home. Place each law on its rung: external conformance at the wire, parsing at the boundary, type on the property class, local law in the property validator, cross-property law in the class validator, cross-object law in the aggregate root, operation legality in the mutator, developer invariants in assertions. Each rung assumes the rungs below and duplicates none. A cheap duplicate deliberately retained for better boundary diagnostics is a documented trade; a law found on two rungs by accident is a bug waiting to be two different laws.
5. Invariants live at the lowest point that sees everything they mention. A channel range belongs to the channel property; a start-before-end rule to the class; unique-ids-across-the-collection to the root that holds the collection. Placing a law lower than its visibility horizon makes it uncheckable; higher, and it runs too often and knows too much.
6. Presence is a four-way decision. Required-at-construction, nullable in the model, defaulted, and omitted-on-serialization are independent axes, and JSON’s omitted / null / empty forms are distinct meanings. Decide per property, record the policy, and never let one optional flag conflate what “the user cleared this” and “the user never touched this.”
7. Constants are identity, not state. If two instances of a class can never differ on a field, the field is part of what the class is: model it as a computed property or inject it at serialization, and keep it out of the constructor. Store it only when round-trip fidelity or spec evolution demands that instances carry it.
8. Represent alternatives as alternatives. Flag fields, mutually exclusive nullables, and mode strings are sum types flattened into products. Give variants honest representation: subclass families when fields or behavior differ, enum properties when only the tag differs, unions for primitive alternatives in one slot. Recover exhaustiveness with loud defaults and registry-driven tests.
9. Inherit for dispatch and substitutability; compose for structure. Parents contribute a property schema and a dispatch position to things that genuinely are the parent. Everything else — nesting, reuse, independent dimensions — is composition. Hierarchies stay shallow: abstract root, concrete leaves, intermediate levels only when they add both schema and a dispatch target. Inherit from a base type only when the object is that primitive.
10. Behavior belongs to generics, and interfaces are generic-sets plus laws. Design the verb vocabulary as deliberately as the class graph. An extension point is a set of generics an implementor must support and the laws those methods must satisfy — write the laws down, executably where possible. Reach for multiple dispatch when behavior genuinely varies along two type axes; it turns a conditionals matrix into small methods.
11. Values in the core, references in the shell. Records of fact are immutable S7 values transformed by pure functions; ongoing processes with identity — sessions, caches, conversations — are R6 or environments at the system’s rim. The domain must be reconstructible from the values alone.
12. Mutate atomically, through the front door. Invariants spanning several properties imply every update of those properties goes through one atomic replacement (S7::set_props()), wrapped in a mutator function so callers cannot do it wrong. Guarantees hold for clients of the exported surface; make the front door the easiest path.
13. One canonical artifact, many projections. When several outputs encode the same knowledge — an expression and a legend; a class graph and its documentation; a wire format and a pretty printer — designate one canonical source (usually a small, reviewable data structure) and generate every projection. Hand-maintained parallel encodings will diverge.
14. Property access is cheap and pure. Getters compute derivations; they never perform I/O, never mutate, never surprise. The moment x@thing can be slow or effectful, the object stops being data in the reader’s mind, and the whole value-semantics reasoning collapses.
15. Abstractions must earn their keep. Every layer of indirection pays rent by absorbing a demonstrated axis of variation — behavioral variation across types, meaning shared across sites, representation churn at a boundary. Abstract after the third occurrence, not the first. Delete layers that no longer pay. The ecosystem’s convergent evolution (independent projects growing the same enum/scalar/presence property helpers) is the positive form of this evidence: those particular abstractions keep earning.
16. Schemas are contracts and inputs, not blueprints. Validate against external schemas with the schema ecosystem’s own tools at the wire; read schemas as a census that informs hand-designed models; generate tables (enums, name maps, requiredness) rather than class graphs. A 1:1 mirror of an external type system imports its structure and discards the chance to encode meaning. And when your own model is the source of truth, store its constraints as data so the schema can be projected from it — one datum, and the validator and the published contract cannot disagree.
17. Refuse to guess. Where no correct behavior is known, an error beats a default. sqlr states the reason perfectly in declining to ship an “ANSI SQL” fallback dialect: an untestable default “would quietly accumulate behaviour no database had ever accepted.” The same logic condemns silent coercion of ambiguous input, fallback branches for “unknown type,” and any code path no test can exercise against a real authority. A loud, early error is information; a guess is deferred corruption.
18. Check as early as the inputs allow, as late as the context requires. The value of a check is proportional to the cost of the work it gates. Declarations should validate themselves at package load (a default violating its own bounds is the author’s bug, catchable before any user exists); configurations should validate fully before the expensive run they configure; and laws that mention context not yet in hand — data dimensions, live resources — should be declared at construction and checked in one named pass at the moment the context arrives, never guessed at and never skipped.
19. Failure travels one of two channels; choose per boundary. Conditions (classed, chained, cli-formatted) are the channel for bugs and contract violations — control flow that should stop. Result-style values are the channel when failure is an expected outcome the caller branches on as data — partial batches, fallible lookups feeding pipelines. Convert between the channels at one designed adapter (resultr’s wrap_in_result() is the model), never with ad hoc tryCatch scattered through the core.

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
section: 9.2 Decision guides
text:
9.2 Decision guides
Formulated as the questions to ask, in order, rather than flowcharts to follow mechanically.
Which object system? Is it fundamentally a homogeneous vector that must slice and live in data frames? — vctrs. Does it have identity and a lifetime, with observers sharing its changes? — R6 or an environment. Is it a domain value with laws and dispatchable behavior? — S7. Is it a veneer for ecosystem politeness? — S3. Mixed answers mean a hybrid, which is normal.
Which sum-type encoding? Do variants differ in fields, or does behavior dispatch on them? — subclass family under an abstract parent. Do they differ only in the tag? — enum-valued property. Is it several primitive shapes lawful in one slot? — union. Is the wire genuinely one bag with conditional fields, variants are many and trivial, and dispatch is never needed? — a discriminator plus class validator, chosen consciously as denormalization.
Which semantic-type tier? Does the concept merely repeat a validation shape across sites? — a reused property definition. Must it be impossible to confuse with its base primitive, or does dispatch need it, while it remains truly a primitive? — a class inheriting the base type. Does it have parts, or operations of its own? — a composite class.
Stored field, identity, or boundary-normalized? Can two instances of the class differ on it? If no — identity (computed property or serializer-injected). If yes — must round-trips preserve the caller’s exact value? If yes — stored, with lenient parsing at the boundary and one canonical stored form. Might the spec extend the value set? — stored enum with a parse-time version gate.
How deep should an embedded language go? Does anything analyze or transform the expressions, or target more than one output format? If no — opaque passthrough, with the engine’s validator as judge. Do humans hand-write the expressions painfully? — constructor combinators (shallow embedding). Is analysis, optimization, or multi-target translation the product? — typed AST with generic passes (deep embedding). Representation as deep as the analysis, and no deeper.

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
section: 9.3 Anti-pattern catalog
text:
9.3 Anti-pattern catalog
Named, so design reviews can point at them.
Schema cosplay. Mirroring an external type system one class per interface. The model inherits every serialization quirk as a nominal type, class count tracks the schema forever, and no semantic layer exists because the schema never had one. Tell: classes whose names and nesting match the wire exactly, none of which ever gains a method.
Validator soup. The same law encoded in the constructor, the property validator, the class validator, and a boundary schema. The encodings drift; error messages disagree; nobody knows which one fired. Tell: fixing one validation bug requires a grep.
Shotgun parsing. Input checks interleaved with processing across many functions, no single point after which input is known-good, rejection possible after side effects. Tell: is.null() and is.character() guards deep in core logic; functions that “defensively” re-check their own package’s objects.
Boolean blindness. Check functions returning TRUE/FALSE whose callers immediately need the why or the what — so they re-derive it. Tell: if (is_valid(x)) { ... } followed by code that re-inspects x for the very facts validity established. Return parsed evidence, not verdicts.
The God validator. One class validator enforcing property-local rules, cross-property rules, and collection rules in a hundred lines. Placement discipline lost; every rung’s law in one place, none assumable by the others. Tell: a class validator that re-checks types.
Convert-everything. Routing lossy, contextual, one-to-many translation through a coercion generic because it exists. Coercion generics (convert(from, to)) suit faithful pairwise conversion; translation with diagnostics, options, and asset generation deserves named functions with room for a context argument and a report. Tell: a convert method with side effects or a dozen options.
Expression-system envy. Re-implementing an engine’s expression type system in property validators — badly, partially, and forever chasing the spec. The engine’s validator owns rung 0. Tell: a validator that walks nested lists interpreting operator names.
Decorative hierarchy. Inheritance introduced to share field names or to “organize” classes that never dispatch differently. Dispatch will eventually take the fake is-a seriously. Tell: an abstract parent with one child, or parents whose children never appear in a method signature.
The mutable domain object. Domain facts held in R6 “for convenience,” surrendering local reasoning, cheap snapshots, and testability to avoid reassignment. Tell: $clone() calls sprinkled defensively; tests full of setup/teardown for what should be a value.
Nullable confusion. NULL doing triple duty as “required but not yet supplied,” “explicitly cleared,” and “omitted on the wire,” with no presence policy. Tell: code that cannot distinguish an untouched field from a cleared one; serializers with ad-hoc per-field if (!is.null()) decisions.
Premature DSL. Combinators, quotation, and clever printing built before any user wrote the target structures by hand long enough to reveal which constructions are actually painful. The DSL then ossifies the wrong abstractions. Tell: a DSL whose vocabulary mirrors the wire format one-to-one instead of the domain’s own idioms.
Effectful getter. A property that reads a file, calls an API, or mutates a cache. Data access becomes action at a distance; cost and effects become invisible at every @. Tell: property access inside a loop dominating a profile; getters needing error handling.
Boundary leakage. Wire names, omit-empty decisions, or dialect quirks appearing in core logic instead of the one serializer pair. Tell: "source-layer" (the wire spelling) as a string anywhere except to_wire()/from_wire().

title: 9  Doctrine: Principles, Decision Guides, and Named Anti-Patterns
section: 9.4 A closing note on judgment
text:
9.4 A closing note on judgment
The principles compress experience, but they trade against each other in real designs: parse-don’t-validate argues for strictness at the boundary while round-trip fidelity argues for permissive pass-through nodes; earned abstraction argues for waiting while semantic atoms argue for naming meanings early; shallow hierarchies argue against intermediate classes while shared schema sometimes argues for them. The earlier documents exist so that when two principles collide, the reasons behind each are available and the trade can be made explicitly, on the record, instead of by whichever slogan was remembered first.

title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
text:
10.1 Finding your playbook
Every other document in this folder is organized by concept — values, types, validation, dispatch, documents. This one is organized by situation. You arrive with a project, not a concept: a published spec to conform to, a pile of TypeScript definitions to interoperate with, an idea for a little language, a training run to configure, a live connection to wrap, an interface others will implement. Each of those situations has a known sequence of opening moves, a known set of traps, and known exemplars in the ecosystem. This document writes those sequences down.
Two references set the genre. Advanced R’s Translating R code chapter (formerly the DSL chapter) teaches domain-specific languages not by theory but by two worked campaigns — an HTML generator and a LaTeX translator — each proceeding from know the target language through build the vocabulary to handle the unknown cases, and each making different design choices for stated reasons. And Tidy design principles covers the “art” register — the naming, argument-design, and ergonomics decisions that no type system settles — as patterns and principles that trade off against one another, to be balanced rather than obeyed. The playbooks below aim for the same registers: sequences of moves that are concrete enough to follow, with the judgment calls flagged as judgment calls.
One orienting fact before the playbooks: they compose. A real package almost never lives inside a single playbook. ellmer runs three at once — wrapping a live resource (the Chat object), modeling wire documents (the Turn/Content graph), and exposing an extension surface (the Provider family). A map-style package runs the spec playbook for the document, the language playbook for embedded expressions, and often the configuration playbook for build options. Identify every playbook in play, because each one places its validation, its state, and its boundaries differently.
Ask where the truth about correctness lives, and what the artifact’s life is:

title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
text:
A published spec, format, or schema exists, and my objects must produce or consume it — Playbook 1. Truth lives outside, in the spec and its official validator.
Type definitions exist in another language — TypeScript, Rust, Go, C, protobuf — and I must mirror or interoperate with them — Playbook 2. Truth lives outside, but in a type system rather than a document format, so the work is translation rather than parsing.
I am inventing the representation: an AST, an IR, a little language — Playbook 3. Truth is yours to define, which is more dangerous than it sounds.
Objects exist to configure computation that happens later, elsewhere, or expensively — Playbook 4. Truth is partly deferred: some laws mention data that does not exist yet.
There is a live thing with a lifetime — a connection, session, device, conversation — Playbook 5. The design problem is drawing the membrane between process and fact.
Other people will implement my classes and generics — Playbook 6. The artifact is the contract itself.

title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
section: 10.2 Playbook 1: Modeling an existing specification
text:
10.2 Playbook 1: Modeling an existing specification
You are here if the domain has a published spec — a map style specification, STAC, GeoJSON, an OpenAPI description, a config file format — and your package’s job is to construct, manipulate, and emit documents that conform to it. This is the document-object-model situation of 06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd, approached now as a sequence of moves rather than an anatomy.

10.2.1 The moves
1. Collect the authorities before writing any code. The spec text, the official machine-readable schema if one exists, the official validator, a reference implementation, and — most valuable of all — a corpus of gold files: real documents produced by the reference tooling, covering the cases you care about. Wire up rung 0 of the checking ladder (the external validator, called mechanically) on day one, because every later decision about what you validate is a decision about what to leave to it.
2. Census the schema; do not transcribe it. This is the schema-as-design-input posture: read the schema as evidence. Count the recurring property shapes (enums, bounded numbers, string-or-expression slots), find the sum types (oneOf with a discriminator, clusters of mutually exclusive optionals), find the deliberately open nodes (additionalProperties, metadata blocks, vendor extensions), and build the requiredness matrix. The census’s output is a page of notes, and that page — not the schema file — is what you design from.
3. Draw the ownership tree, then the reference edges, then pick the root. Composition edges become nested properties; symbolic references (a layer names a source by id) become the referential-integrity laws that will live on the aggregate root’s validator. The root is the unit of consistency, serialization, and external validation.
4. Name the semantic atoms and collapse the structural duplicates. The spec’s type definitions will contain many structurally distinct spellings of one meaning (the proverbial fifteen colors). One semantic type per meaning, per the tiers of 03-types-and-meaning.qmd, regardless of how many shapes the wire uses.
5. Build one vertical slice before broadening. Pick a single leaf node and take it all the way: class, boundary parser, serializer, presence policy, round-trip test against a gold file. The slice forces every infrastructure decision — wire-name mapping, omit-empty policy, unknown-key policy, the equivalence relation your round-trip law uses — while the stakes are one class instead of forty. Only then fan out across the node catalog, which by that point is mostly mechanical.
6. Decide presence per property and openness per node, on the record. The four presence axes (required, nullable, defaulted, omitted) and the open/closed decision are the two choices that cannot be retrofitted cheaply. Strict where you claim semantics; pass-through where the spec is deliberately extensible.
7. Meet users at the objects they already hold. The best boundary constructors lift native objects into the model — stacbuildr’s item_from_terra() builds STAC items from rasters, not from hand-assembled metadata lists. Ask what your users have in their hands before you ask them to learn your class graph.


10.2.2 A slice, worked
The smallest complete slice — one node, one parser, one serializer, one law (verified against S7 0.2.2):
to_wire <- S7::new_generic("to_wire", "x")

vector_source <- S7::new_class("vector_source", properties = list(
  url         = S7::class_character,
  min_zoom    = S7::new_property(S7::class_numeric, default = 0),
  attribution = S7::new_property(
    S7::new_union(S7::class_character, NULL), default = NULL
  )
))

source_from_wire <- function(json) {
  # the boundary owns wire names, defaults, and coercion, once
  vector_source(
    url         = json[["url"]],
    min_zoom    = json[["minzoom"]] %||% 0,
    attribution = json[["attribution"]]
  )
}

S7::method(to_wire, vector_source) <- function(x) {
  out <- list(type = "vector", url = x@url)   # 'type' is identity, injected
  if (x@min_zoom != 0) out[["minzoom"]] <- x@min_zoom
  if (!is.null(x@attribution)) out[["attribution"]] <- x@attribution
  out
}
Small as it is, the slice already embodies five decisions: the wire spelling minzoom exists in exactly two functions; the type constant is identity, not a stored property; attribution is nullable and omitted when absent (two axes, decided separately); the default min_zoom is omitted on the wire (so the round-trip law must be canonical equality, not byte identity); and the parser is the only path in. Scaling to the full spec is repetition of this shape, which is exactly why the slice comes first.


10.2.3 Traps
Schema cosplay (transcribing the schema instead of censusing it), expression-system envy (re-implementing the engine’s validator for embedded expressions — see Playbook 3 for what to do instead), and validator soup (your rungs re-checking what the official validator already owns). All three are named in the anti-pattern catalog.
Exemplars: stacbuildr (the pattern complete), rapid (an OpenAPI spec as a strict domain object), S7schema (rung 0 productized), typedjson (the round trip as the entire product). See 07-ecosystem-field-guide.qmd, Cluster B.
