title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
section: 10.3 Playbook 2: Translating foreign type definitions
text:
10.3 Playbook 2: Translating foreign type definitions
You are here if the source of truth is a type system rather than a document format: a TypeScript definition file, Rust or Go structs, C headers, protobuf messages. The deliverable is different from Playbook 1’s — not a parser for documents but a correspondence between two type systems, and the central artifact is a translation table you write before any class.

10.3.1 The moves
1. Write the translation table first. Every foreign construct gets a row: what it is there, what it becomes here, and what is lost or gained in the crossing. The table below covers the recurring rows; your table adds the domain-specific ones. The discipline matters because translation decisions made ad hoc, class by class, drift — the same TS string | null becomes three different presence policies in three files.



Foreign construct
S7 move
Watch for




TS interface / struct
hand-designed class, after collapsing structural duplicates
serialization artifacts posing as domain objects


tagged union (TS discriminated union, Rust enum with payloads, protobuf oneof)
abstract parent + subclass family; the tag is class identity
flattening it into one bag with a mode string


TS string-literal union ("a" \| "b")
validated enum property (or a formalized enum class)
modeling it as a free character


TS field?: T vs field: T \| null vs field: T \| undefined
three different presence decisions on the four axes
collapsing all three to one NULL


Rust Option<T>
NULL union member plus an explicit presence policy
—


Rust Result<T, E>
conditions, or resultr values, per doctrine 19
mirroring it structurally without choosing a channel


Rust newtype (struct Meters(f64))
semantic type: base-type-inheriting class or reused property, per tier
dropping it to a bare double


Go zero values
explicit defaults + presence policy
conflating “absent” with “zero”


Go embedded struct / TS extends
composition first; a parent class only if is-a is honest
decorative hierarchy


generics (Vec<T>, Array<T>, Map<K,V>)
list property + membership validator; element type documented and enforced, not parametric
pretending S7 has parametric types (it does not)


TS utility types (Partial<T>, Pick<T, K>)
do not mirror; they are structural derivations — re-derive at the boundary if needed
one class per derived shape


protobuf unknown fields / extensions
inert pass-through bag with key discipline
interpreting bag contents in core logic



2. Sort every foreign type into transport or domain. The foreign definitions almost always mix both: types that exist because the wire needed a shape, and types that carry the domain’s actual concepts. The transport stratum may be mirrored mechanically (the generated transport model of 06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd) — labeled as transport and kept behind boundary parsers. The domain stratum is hand-designed from the census, exactly as in Playbook 1. The whole failure mode of this playbook is letting the first stratum stand in for the second.
3. Fix the interop direction, because it places the parsing. If you consume their values (their runtime serializes, you deserialize), your boundary is a parser and the certificate is yours to mint. If you produce values for their runtime, their validator is rung 0 and your serializer must satisfy it — which usually means gold files generated by their tooling and a conformance test that runs their checker if it is invocable. Bidirectional interop means both, plus a round-trip law with a named equivalence relation.
4. Import the laws, not just the shapes. Foreign type systems encode some invariants you cannot see in the type text: Rust’s ownership rules mean an &mut parameter is a promise about aliasing that R cannot state; TS’s readonly is a promise S7 can approximate with a write-once setter or simply by value semantics. Read the foreign documentation for the laws that live outside the types, and give them homes on the ladder — they are the part a mechanical translation silently drops.


10.3.2 Traps
The deadliest is assuming their equality and their nullability idioms transfer. Two structurally equal Go structs are ==-comparable; two S7 objects are compared however you define comparison, and until you define it, identical() — representational identity — is all you have, which is almost never the contract the foreign code meant. Likewise undefined versus null versus absent-key is a real distinction in a TS codebase and a single NULL in naive R translation. Both are presence-policy and equality-relation decisions (06) that the translation table must settle globally, not per class.
Exemplars: rapid (OpenAPI’s component types as a strict S7 substrate), the R-ArcGIS stack (Esri’s JSON types over s7x foundations), structr (the contrast: when fidelity to a schema is the product and no domain layer is wanted, a compiled non-S7 schema engine is honest about that).

title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
section: 10.4 Playbook 3: Building a language from scratch
text:
10.4 Playbook 3: Building a language from scratch
You are here if no external spec constrains you: you are designing an AST, a compiler IR, a query builder, an expression vocabulary — a little language whose truth you define. This is the most seductive playbook, because R’s metaprogramming makes language-building nearly frictionless and S7’s variant families make ASTs pleasant; the discipline is the escalation ladder of 06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd, climbed slowly.

10.4.1 The moves
1. Write the target artifact by hand until it hurts. The Advanced R translation chapter’s silent first lesson: both case studies begin with the author fluent in the target language (HTML, LaTeX), writing target output manually, before any R vocabulary exists. The pain points of manual writing are the requirements list for the DSL; a DSL designed before the pain is felt ossifies the wrong abstractions (the premature-DSL anti-pattern). If nobody has hand-written the nested lists your combinators will generate, you do not yet know which constructions need help.
2. Default to rung 1 and demand justification for each climb. Opaque passthrough — store the expression as a list or string, let the engine judge it — is the correct default, not a temporary embarrassment. Climb to rung 2 (constructor combinators) when humans demonstrably suffer writing the raw form. Climb to rung 3 (a typed AST) only when analysis or multi-target translation is the product.
3. At rung 2, name the vocabulary after the domain’s idioms, not the wire’s grammar. A combinator layer that mirrors the wire one-to-one adds spelling safety and nothing else. The valuable combinators are the ones that compress an idiom — expr_interpolate(zoom, stops) rather than a transliteration of the underlying operator tree. This is where Tidy design principles does the most work: enumerate the possible options in arguments, required arguments without defaults, prefer an enum over two booleans, put the data argument first. Combinators are functions; function-design craft is DSL craft.
4. At rung 3, the shape is fixed: closed variant family, smart constructors, passes as generics. An abstract node root, concrete leaf nodes, constructors that reject unlawful nodes at build time, and — the part functional OOP uniquely rewards — every operation over the tree is a generic, so each new analysis is a new generic with per-node methods, not an edit to the node classes. This is the expression problem resolved in the direction a language wants: the node set is closed and stable; the operation set is open and growing.
5. Write the printer immediately after the nodes. A language whose values cannot render themselves readably is undebuggable, and the printer doubles as the first real pass — writing it forces you to walk every node kind once, which surfaces structural mistakes while the family is still small. (In S7 terms: a format() method per node, before any clever pass.)
6. Decide the surface syntax last: constructors or quoted R. Two different products. Constructor syntax (cmp("==", "class", "park")) is ordinary code — honest, pipeable, no magic. Quoted-R syntax (filter(class == "park")) makes R itself the surface language via quotation, which is strictly more powerful and strictly more dangerous: you inherit R’s grammar for free and its ambiguity forever. The Advanced R LaTeX case study shows the cost concretely — a translator over quoted R must decide what every unknown symbol means, and the honest options are translate-known / error-unknown (refuse to guess, doctrine 17) or an explicit escape hatch, never silent passthrough. quickr is the full-scale version: R source with declare(type()) annotations, parsed into a typed S7 IR, passes over the IR, Fortran out. Choose quotation when your users should think in R; choose constructors when they should think in your domain’s nouns.


10.4.2 A rung-3 core, worked
The minimal honest AST — abstract root, two nodes, two passes — verified against S7 0.2.2:
filter_expr <- S7::new_class("filter_expr", abstract = TRUE)

cmp <- S7::new_class("cmp", parent = filter_expr, properties = list(
  op = S7::new_property(S7::class_character, validator = function(value) {
    if (length(value) != 1 || !value %in% c("==", "!=", "<", ">")) {
      "must be one of ==, !=, <, >"
    }
  }),
  field = S7::class_character,
  value = S7::class_any
))

all_of <- S7::new_class("all_of", parent = filter_expr, properties = list(
  exprs = S7::new_property(S7::class_list, validator = function(value) {
    if (!all(vapply(value, S7::S7_inherits, logical(1), class = filter_expr))) {
      "every element must be a filter_expr"
    }
  })
))

# each pass is a new generic; the node family never changes
to_wire <- S7::new_generic("to_wire", "x")
S7::method(to_wire, cmp)    <- function(x) list(x@op, x@field, x@value)
S7::method(to_wire, all_of) <- function(x) c(list("all"), lapply(x@exprs, to_wire))

fields_used <- S7::new_generic("fields_used", "x")
S7::method(fields_used, cmp)    <- function(x) x@field
S7::method(fields_used, all_of) <- function(x)
  unique(unlist(lapply(x@exprs, fields_used)))
The second pass is the entire justification for rung 3: fields_used() is an analysis — something a stored list could never answer without being re-parsed. If no such pass exists in your plans, to_wire() alone does not justify the nodes; stay at rung 2 and emit lists directly.


10.4.3 Traps
Premature DSL (move 1 skipped), representation deeper than analysis (rung 3 with one serializing consumer), and — for quoted surfaces — evaluating user text (eval(parse()) is never the mechanism; quotation and walking are). Exhaustiveness is the structural weak point of R’s closed families: a new node kind will not force old passes to update, so keep a registry of node classes and a test asserting every pass has a method for every node.
Exemplars: quickr (rung 3 as a product: the IR is the compiler), sqlr (a schema language whose passes are renderers per dialect), dbplyr in S3 terms, and the Advanced R chapter’s two case studies as the genre’s teaching texts.

title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
section: 10.5 Playbook 4: Configuring expensive computation
text:
10.5 Playbook 4: Configuring expensive computation
You are here if your objects exist to parameterize work — a model training run, a rendering job, a deployment — and the gap between “config written” and “consequence discovered” is minutes, hours, or money. The organizing principle is doctrine 18: check as early as the inputs allow, as late as the context requires. rtemis is the fully worked exhibit.

10.5.1 The moves
1. One class per decision cluster; compose the clusters. A hyperparameter set, a resampling policy, a preprocessing pipeline — each is its own small class with its own laws, composed into the run configuration. The alternative (one flat bag of forty fields) has no place to put cross-field laws and no way to reuse a cluster across contexts.
2. The constructor is a parser with opinions. Enumerate options (match.arg-style, or an enum property), refuse required arguments with defaults, refuse to guess on ambiguity. Tidy design’s argument canon applies with extra force here because a configuration constructor is the single point where a human’s intent becomes machine-checkable — every leniency in it is a deferred debugging session.
3. Validate everything validatable at setup time, before the expensive thing. The setup_*() pattern: a fully validated configuration object is minted before the run, so a typo costs milliseconds. The object is a certificate; the run function demands the class and re-checks nothing.
4. Declare context-dependent laws as data; resolve them in one named pass. Some laws mention what does not exist yet — mtry bounded by the number of features, weights matching the number of rows. Declare these on the property as data (rtemis’s data_bound), and check them in one explicit resolution step at the moment the data arrives. Never smuggle them into a validator that would have to guess, and never skip them because construction-time checking was impossible.
5. Make the configuration readable back. A print method that shows the resolved state — supplied values, applied defaults, deferred checks still pending — is not cosmetics; it is the only way a user can confirm the certificate says what they meant before spending the compute. A config that cannot be inspected will be re-specified from scratch every time doubt arises, which defeats its purpose as a value.


10.5.2 Traps
The flat god-config (move 1 skipped); silent defaults for consequential choices (an untestable default “quietly accumulates behaviour no database had ever accepted” — sqlr’s phrase generalizes to every default nobody chose); and validating at run time what was knowable at setup time, which converts cheap errors into expensive ones at exactly the moment the user is least able to iterate.
Exemplars: rtemis (setup_*() + data_bound, Cluster D of the field guide), optimizers7 (stopping rules as composable configuration objects).

title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
section: 10.6 Playbook 5: Wrapping a live resource
text:
10.6 Playbook 5: Wrapping a live resource
You are here if the domain contains something with a lifetime — a database connection, an HTTP session, a browser, a device handle, an accumulating conversation. Value semantics cannot model it, because its whole point is that observers share its changes. The design problem is not “how do I make S7 mutable” (you don’t) but where to draw the membrane between the process and the facts it produces.

10.6.1 The moves
1. Sort every noun into fact or process. Facts — a completed turn, a query result, a fitted model, a snapshot of settings — are S7 values. Processes — the connection, the session, the accumulating history — get reference semantics: R6 or an environment. The sort is the design; ellmer is its exhibit (mutable R6 Chat, immutable S7 Turn/Content crossing the membrane in both directions).
2. Keep the reference object thin: lifecycle and orchestration only. Everything computable belongs in pure functions over the value types, called by the process object. The test is direct: if a method’s logic can be tested without standing up the live resource, it should not live on the reference class. This is functional core / imperative shell with the shell given a name and a lifetime.
3. Values in, values out. The reference object’s methods accept S7 values and return S7 values. State never leaks out as a shared mutable structure; callers get facts, not handles into the internals. Where a property of an S7 value must hold a reference (a cache, a connection), remember the law from 02-values-and-state.qmd: value semantics is only as deep as the payload — document it, exclude it from equality and serialization, or snapshot it.
4. Make provider variation a dispatch surface, not a conditional. When the live resource comes in flavors (LLM providers, database backends, tile services), the flavor is an S7 value the process object holds, and behavior varies by methods on generics over it. This is ellmer’s Provider design and sqlr’s dialect dispatch: the reference object stays one class; the variation lives in the value world where dispatch works.
5. Every important state must project to values. A snapshot() / as_data() path from the process to plain values is what makes the system testable, persistable, and debuggable. If some state cannot be projected, that state cannot be asserted on in a test — which usually means it is about to become folklore.


10.6.2 Traps
The mutable domain object (facts stored in R6 “for convenience” — anti-pattern catalog); the fat session class that accretes every function that ever needed the connection; and the leaked handle — returning internal mutable state to callers who then observe changes they never subscribed to.
Exemplars: ellmer (the hybrid architecture, Cluster A of the field guide); tooey for the fully inverted variant, where the framework owns the entire shell and user code is pure.

title: 10  Playbooks: How to Approach S7, by Situation
section: 10.7 Playbook 6: Designing a surface others extend
text:
10.7 Playbook 6: Designing a surface others extend
You are here if the point of the package is that strangers implement it: storage backends, model engines, providers, format plugins. In functional OOP the extension surface is a set of generics plus the laws their methods must satisfy — the interface is implicit in S7, so the work of this playbook is making it explicit enough to implement against.

10.7.1 The moves
1. Verbs before nouns. Draft the generic vocabulary first — the operations every implementation must support — and write the law each generic carries (store_read() after store_write() returns what was written; render() is pure; close() is idempotent). The abstract root class exists to give dispatch a place to stand; the vocabulary and laws are the actual interface.
2. Build two implementations before freezing anything. One real, one toy (an in-memory fake living in the test suite). The second implementor is where every accidental assumption of the first gets discovered — a generic whose signature only makes sense for the filesystem backend, a law that was really an implementation detail. An interface with one implementation is a speculation, not an abstraction (doctrine 15).
3. Export the conformance suite as a function. A test_backend_conformance(backend) that any implementor can run against their class converts the written laws into executable ones. s7contract shows the machinery (contracts, traits, generative laws with shrinking); even without machinery, a plain testthat function over the generic vocabulary is the single highest-leverage artifact this playbook produces.
4. Make capabilities optional by declaration, not by error. When some implementations support an operation and others cannot, add a capability predicate generic (supports_streaming(x)) with a default of FALSE, and let the framework branch on it — rather than requiring every implementor to stub methods that throw. This is interface evolution’s front door: new capabilities arrive as new optional generics with safe defaults, and old implementations keep working unchanged (05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd).
5. Version the contract in words. State which generics are required, which are optional, and what a conforming implementation may assume about call order and argument validity (typically: the framework validates inputs, so methods may trust them — say so). Silence here means every implementor re-validates defensively, which is shotgun parsing distributed across an ecosystem.


10.7.2 Traps
The speculative interface (one implementation, frozen API); the leaky root (an abstract parent whose properties encode one backend’s needs); and law-free generics — a vocabulary with no stated laws is an interface in syntax only, and implementations will satisfy the signatures while diverging on every behavior that matters.
Exemplars: objectstore (interface-first, embryonic and explicit about it), ellmer’s Provider family (the mature version, with the framework owning orchestration), s7contract (laws made executable).

section: 10.8 Combining playbooks: two worked identifications
text:
10.8 Combining playbooks: two worked identifications
A map-style package. The style document is Playbook 1 (spec, gold files, aggregate root, one serializer pair). Embedded filter and paint expressions are Playbook 3, entered at rung 1 and climbed only if legend generation or expression analysis becomes a product requirement (that analysis pass — fields_used() above — is precisely the justification test). Build options, if any, are a small Playbook 4. Nothing here is Playbook 5: a style is a value through and through, and the moment a “style manager” R6 class appears, a wrong turn has been taken.
An API client with typed payloads. The session — auth, retries, rate limits — is Playbook 5 (a thin reference shell over httr2). The request/response payloads are Playbook 2 if the provider publishes types (translation table, transport/domain sort) or Playbook 1 if it publishes an OpenAPI document. If the client is meant to support multiple provider backends, the provider abstraction is Playbook 6, and the conformance suite is what keeps the third-party backend honest.
The identification step is worth doing explicitly at project start, because the playbooks disagree about where checking lives (the spec’s validator versus your constructors versus a deferred resolution pass), where state is allowed (nowhere versus the named shell), and what the first artifact should be (a gold-file corpus, a translation table, a hand-written target document, a conformance suite). Knowing which game each part of the system is playing is most of what “architecture” means at this scale.
One caveat about what playbooks are: they are opening theory. They get a project through its first decisions in the right order; they cannot show how those decisions interact ten moves later, when the presence policy constrains the round-trip law and the spec’s churn rate argues against the sum-type encoding the doctrine recommends. That layer — the middlegame — is 10-middlegame.qmd, which traces the pressure chains of the mature packages and plays one design derivation out in full, concessions included.

title: 11  The Middlegame: From Doctrine to a Real Package
text:
11.1 The gap this document exists to close
Be honest about what the folder contained before this document. The conceptual chapters justify a worldview. The doctrine compresses it into defaults. The field guide shows positions — snapshots of finished packages with the pattern each one exhibits. The playbooks give opening theory — the first eight moves for six recognizable situations. In chess terms, the collection had openings, annotated positions, and endgame tables, and was missing the genre that actually teaches judgment: annotated full games, where you watch the decisions get made in sequence, interacting, under pressure, with the alternatives visible and the concessions priced.
The gap is structural, not editorial. Doctrine is stated per decision — one principle, one rung, one encoding choice at a time — but a real package is a system of coupled decisions: the presence policy constrains the round-trip law, which constrains the open/closed choice, which feeds back into what the validators may assume. Toy examples cannot exhibit coupling, because coupling only appears when there are enough decisions to couple. This is why the mature packages — ellmer, ragnar, quickr, rtemis — feel categorically more complicated than anything in the playbooks: they are not applying more patterns; they are absorbing the interactions.
So this document does two things. First it re-reads the mature four, not for their patterns (the field guide’s job) but for their pressure chains — the sequence by which one hard requirement forced a cascade of design consequences, including the concessions. Then it plays one annotated game at realistic fidelity: a style-document core, derived decision by decision, with the doctrine cited where it was followed and overruled where reality outvoted it. The code for the load-bearing spine was verified against S7 0.2.2 on R 4.6.1.

title: 11  The Middlegame: From Doctrine to a Real Package
section: 11.2 Part I: How the mature four absorbed complexity
text:
11.2 Part I: How the mature four absorbed complexity

11.2.1 ellmer: one requirement forces the hybrid
The instructive way to read ellmer is to ask what forced each piece of its architecture, and the answer starts with a product requirement, not a philosophy: streaming. A streamed response is a value that does not exist yet — tokens accumulate over seconds, consumers want them as they arrive, and the eventual Turn is only a fact once the stream closes. Partial state must live somewhere, and no amount of value-semantics conviction changes that. That single requirement makes the mutable Chat object load-bearing: R6 is not a stylistic lapse but the honest home for an accumulation-in-progress, and the doctrine’s actual contribution is containment — completed turns crystallize into immutable S7 values, the conversation is reconstructible from the values alone, and the mutable rim stays one class wide.
The second chain: provider variation. Every supported provider has quirks — capabilities, wire formats, authentication, streaming protocols — and the Provider dispatch surface absorbs them. The price, visible if you watch the package evolve, is that a plugin surface grows: each new provider capability becomes a new generic or a new argument somewhere, and the interface can never again be reorganized cheaply because third parties stand on it. The lesson for the middlegame: doctrine 10 tells you to design the verb vocabulary carefully; ellmer shows why the stakes are asymmetric — under-designing an internal function costs a refactor, under-designing an extension surface costs an ecosystem migration.


11.2.2 ragnar: the price tag on base-type inheritance
The compendium praises MarkdownDocumentChunks inheriting from tibble as “honest base-type inheritance” — the value really is a table. The middlegame reading adds the invoice: inheriting a base type means the parent’s entire API becomes your unvalidated mutator set. Every dplyr verb, every [ method, every tool in the tibble ecosystem can transform the object along paths where the subclass’s laws are never consulted — drop the columns the class depends on, break the alignment with @document, or silently strip the subclass entirely. ragnar’s concession is that its invariants on that surface are documented rather than enforced, and re-established at the operations that matter. That is a rational trade — the whole point of inheriting tibble is to get that ecosystem — but it is a trade, and the doctrine’s “construction is the proof” holds only on the package’s own front doors, not on the thousand side doors the parent class ships with. When you inherit a base type, you are choosing which of those doors to guard, and accepting the rest.


11.2.3 quickr: power through refusal
quickr compiles R to Fortran, and the design decision that makes it possible is what it declines: it accepts a subset of R, requires declare(type()) annotations, and errors on constructs it cannot compile faithfully rather than approximating their semantics. This is doctrine 17 — refuse to guess — applied not to an argument default but to the entire domain of the tool: shrink the promise until you can keep it. The middlegame lesson generalizes to every “model an existing thing” project: the fastest route to a robust core is usually not handling more of the input space, it is drawing a smaller boundary you can defend completely, with loud errors at the fence. Coverage grows later, fence post by fence post, each one tested. The packages that tried to accept everything on day one are the ones whose validators are full of guesses.


11.2.4 rtemis: the fixed cost of constraints-as-data
rtemis’s property-factory stratum — the PropertySpec machinery deriving validators, defaults, JSON Schema, and TUI forms from single declarations — is the compendium’s favorite exhibit for constraints-as-data. The middlegame reading prices it: that stratum is itself a serious system, hundreds of lines of meta-machinery that every contributor must understand before they can add a property, and every error message now has an extra layer of indirection between the symptom and the declaration. It amortizes because rtemis has hundreds of hyperparameters across dozens of models and genuinely needs all four projections. Below some scale threshold — and most packages are below it — hand-written new_property() calls are not a failure to apply the pattern; they are the pattern correctly not applied (doctrine 15: the third occurrence, not the first). The factory stratum is the right move exactly when you can name the projections you need and count the declarations that will pay for it.


11.2.5 The shared shape
Four packages, one shape: each met a pressure that made the naive, doctrine-by-the-letter design uneconomic — streaming broke pure values, ecosystem reuse broke enforced invariants, R’s full semantics broke compilability, hyperparameter count broke hand-written validation. And each responded the same way: not by abandoning a principle but by moving where it applies — containing state instead of forbidding it, guarding chosen doors instead of all doors, shrinking the promise instead of diluting it, buying machinery only where the census showed volume. That move — relocating a principle’s jurisdiction instead of revoking it — is the core middlegame skill, and it is exactly what per-decision doctrine cannot teach and an annotated game can.

section: 11.4 Part III: The loop that actually transfers the wisdom
text:
11.4 Part III: The loop that actually transfers the wisdom
The last honest thing this document can say is that no document — not this one — converts wisdom into skill. The mature four were not designed by consulting a compendium; they were designed by people making decisions, hitting walls, and revising. What a compendium can do is shorten that loop: make the decision points visible sooner, the options nameable, and the concessions explicit instead of accidental. The transfer mechanism is a practice, and it is cheap:
Keep a design journal in the project. One entry per real decision, five lines: the decision, the pressure, the options considered, the choice, and the principle followed or overruled, with the reason. The annotated game above is exactly this journal, written after the fact; writing it during the fact is faster and truer. The journal does two jobs at once: it makes “selectively considering the proper aspects” an explicit act instead of an anxiety (you consulted the doctrine, you cited or overruled it, done — no lingering doubt about whether you should have used some sophisticated pattern you decided against), and it produces the evidence stream the compendium needs to stay alive — a recurring overrule in your journals is a counterexample entry for open-questions.qmd, and a pattern that keeps earning across your projects is a promotion candidate.
Review the journal at complexity checkpoints, not on a schedule. The natural checkpoints: the first mutator (is the invariant placement holding?), the first serializer (did presence and equality get decided together?), the tenth class (is a factory stratum starting to amortize?), the first external implementor (is the interface really a contract?). These are the moments the middlegame pressure chains start, and a half-hour against the doctrine’s decision guides at each one is worth more than any amount of up-front design piety.
That is the whole method: openings from the playbooks, this document’s annotated game as the model for the middlegame, the journal as your own annotation habit, and the ledger as the place your games feed back into the theory. Eating our own food is not a property the compendium can have by itself — it is a loop the compendium and the projects run together.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
A.1 Working hypotheses: patterns with one source
Everything else in this folder records what the investigation concluded. This document records what it did not: hypotheses resting on a single data point, S7 behaviors that may shift under the compendium’s feet, design tensions the doctrine acknowledges but does not resolve, and the standing requests for evidence — especially contrary evidence — that would change a recommendation. A living compendium that keeps only its conclusions slowly forgets why it believes them; this ledger is the hedge against that.
Entries move in both directions. When new evidence promotes a hypothesis, it graduates into the numbered documents and is struck here. When a counterexample lands, it is recorded here first, and the relevant doctrine is amended second — never silently.
Each of these is treated in the main documents as a real pattern, and each currently rests on a single package. Recurrence in a second independent project would promote it to a convergent pattern; failure to recur, or a discovered flaw, demotes it.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
text:
Write-once property setters as tamper-evidence for certificate-like fields (resultr). Open question: how robust is setter-based enforcement, given that attributes remain reachable by other means and copies re-run setters in some paths? A second sighting, or a demonstrated bypass that matters in practice, would settle its standing.
One designed adapter between the condition channel and the value channel (resultr’s wrap_in_result()). The principle (doctrine 19) is derived and stands on general reasoning; the single-adapter discipline specifically has one exhibit.
Model-View-Update as a whole-program S7 architecture (tooey). The claim that MVU answers “where do events go?” for value-oriented R designs generalizes beyond terminal UIs — but nobody has yet done it beyond terminal UIs.
Constraints-as-data driving four projections from one declaration (rtemis: validator, default, JSON Schema, TUI form). The reverse arrow itself has a second exhibit (sqlr’s DDL/diff/reflect projections), but the full property-spec-to-many-artifacts machine is a single sighting.
A metaobject descriptor layer — reflection productized as immutable descriptor objects (datarr/reflect). The underlying fact (classes are data) is documented mechanism; the usefulness of a dedicated descriptor package is hypothesis.
Interface-first design with the implementations deferred (objectstore, which is explicit about being a bet). This one is self-declared unresolved: the interesting datum will be whether the interface survives its first two real backends unchanged.

section: A.2 The S7 watch list: version-anchored facts
text:
A.2 The S7 watch list: version-anchored facts
S7 is at 0.2.x. The compendium’s verified mechanics are anchored to S7 0.2.2 on R 4.6.1, and several could legitimately change:

Validator invocation counts — once per construction, once per @<- replacement (affected property only), once per set_props() batch. Optimizations here would change the cost model’s arithmetic but not its structure.
Copy behavior under @<- — currently a full shallow copy per replacement, observable via tracemem(). Any future in-place optimization for singly-referenced objects would change the observable mechanics while (probably) preserving the semantics; the two-binding divergence test is the invariant to re-run, not the tracemem() output.
The object representation itself — properties as attributes, the class definition embedded in each instance under the S7_class attribute (see the evolution section below; this one has large consequences if it changes).
S4 interop, convert(), and super() semantics — used lightly in the compendium, but worth re-verifying at each S7 release.
Possible future features that would retire current advice: sealed classes or any native exhaustiveness checking would obsolete the registry-driven exhaustiveness tests recommended in 05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd; a load-time revalidation hook would rewrite the evolution guidance below.

On the R side, the value-semantics story rests on the post-4.0 reference counter’s behavior (including its one-sided approximations, which we verified can strand counts high in IDE sessions). ALTREP expansion or refcounting changes would warrant re-running the probe suite.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.3 Unresolved design tensions
text:
A.3 Unresolved design tensions
The doctrine’s closing note admits the principles collide; these are the collisions where the ledger does not yet know the resolution conditions.

Boundary strictness versus round-trip fidelity. Open nodes (pass-through bags) buy fidelity for foreign content at the cost of weaker guarantees. The doctrine says “choose per node, on the record” — but the conditions under which an open node’s weaker guarantee becomes unacceptable (security boundary? multi-writer round trips?) are not characterized.
Semantic atoms early versus abstraction earned by the rule of three. Naming meanings early is doctrine 1; waiting for the third occurrence is doctrine 15. They directly disagree about timing, and the current resolution (“meaning is different from machinery”) is a judgment call, not a rule.
One authoritative home versus diagnostic duplicates. The revised doctrine 4 permits a “cheap, documented duplicate” for better boundary errors. How many is too many, and what makes a duplicate cheap enough? Unquantified.
Enum property versus subclass family at the margin. The decision guide is clear at the extremes; the margin — variants differing in one optional field, or in behavior for exactly one generic — still gets decided by taste.
Aggregate-root granularity in deep documents. When a document is five levels deep with cross-references at three of them, is there one root or nested roots with delegated validators? The DDD literature says aggregates should be small; document trees resist that. Unresolved.
Value purity versus practical caching. A derived value worth memoizing wants a reference cell inside a value, which 02-values-and-state.qmd correctly flags as piercing value semantics. Snapshot-or-document is the current answer; a blessed cache pattern (compute-at-construction? external memo table keyed by content?) has not been worked out.

section: A.4 Counterexamples wanted
text:
A.4 Counterexamples wanted
A standing collection protocol. The field guide selects successes and extracts patterns from them; that is a sampling bias, and the correction is to record, whenever encountered:

A design that violates the doctrine and works well anyway.
A project that adopted S7 and retreated (to S3, R6, or plain lists), with the stated reasons.
A case where the flattened transport model beat semantic modeling on total cost — including maintenance, not just initial build.
A case where duplicated validation earned its diagnostics for years without drifting.
A case where an R6 domain model was simpler and safer than the pure value core it replaced or prevented.
A typed AST that was collapsed back to combinators, and what the collapse cost.

Each entry should record what happened, which pressure the doctrine missed, and which principle (if any) should gain a stated exception. None exist in the ledger yet — which after one day is expected, and after one year would itself be evidence of not looking.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.5 The object-evolution frontier
text:
A.5 The object-evolution frontier
The largest open architectural topic: what happens when S7 values become persisted records and outlive their class definitions. Initial probes (S7 0.2.2, R 4.6.1) establish the mechanics, and they are sharp-edged:

The class definition travels inside every object. An S7 instance carries its full class object — property list, validator closures, constructor — in its S7_class attribute, and saveRDS() serializes all of it. A one-property object’s reachable graph measured ~37 KB against ~340 B for the equivalent bare list; per-file overhead of that order applies to every individually serialized value.
Reloaded objects pass identity checks against redefined classes. After redefining a class (new required property, new validator), a reloaded old-shape object still satisfies S7_inherits() — identity is by class name, not structure. New methods therefore dispatch on old objects and fail only when they touch the missing property (Can't find property <evo_cls>@b), mid-operation.
S7::validate() runs the embedded, stale validator. The reloaded object validates against the class definition it carries, not the current one. Load-time revalidation against the live class does not happen and cannot be requested from S7 today.

The pattern of these three facts: version skew is silent at the boundary and loud in the middle — the exact inversion of everything 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd argues for. Which makes the working hypothesis, recorded here for future testing:

rds is a cache format, not a persistence format. Serialized S7 objects are trustworthy only within a single class-definition version — same session, same package version, same process family. Durable persistence should travel the wire channel (to_wire() / from_wire()), because the parser re-validates against the current class on entry, version-gates explicitly, and pays none of the embedded class-definition overhead.

Open questions beneath the hypothesis:

Should classes intended for persistence carry an explicit schema-version property, with from_wire() dispatching migration (upgrade_v1_to_v2()) on it? (This is standard practice elsewhere; no S7 package has been observed doing it yet.)
Do pass-through extension bags actually survive multiple read-modify-write cycles in practice, or do intermediate normalizations quietly drop foreign keys? (Testable against stacbuildr or a local document model.)
What are the compatibility expectations across package releases — is a serialized object from version N a supported input to version N+1, and who documents that? (Currently: nobody, implicitly no.)
Does the embedded class definition capture environments through validator closures, and can that leak surprising amounts of data into rds files? (The measured 37 KB suggests yes; unexamined.)

section: A.6 Targeted cost questions
text:
A.6 Targeted cost questions
The cost model in 04-parse-dont-validate.qmd is architectural, not measured, and that is probably sufficient. If measurement ever becomes worthwhile, these are the specific decisions to weigh — not a generic “is S7 fast” benchmark:

Bulk construction: constructor-per-element versus valid_eventually()-batched, at 10^4 to 10^6 nodes.
Multi-property update: set_props() versus sequential @<-, wall time (validator counts are already verified: one versus per-assignment).
Copy cost of nested graphs: the shallow-copy probes imply replacement cost tracks top-level property count while payloads share structure; unverified at document scale.
Dispatch overhead versus S3 in hot loops — relevant to rung-3 AST passes, where every node visit is a generic call.
Load-time cost of property-factory strata at rtemis scale (their factory-time validation trades startup cost for author safety; the price is unmeasured).
Serialized-corpus overhead of embedded class definitions (single-object anchor measured above; corpus-scale unexamined).

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.7 S7-specific, or merely illustrated with S7?
text:
A.7 S7-specific, or merely illustrated with S7?
An unperformed classification pass: for each doctrine principle, would it survive a substrate change to, say, Python dataclasses with pydantic, or TypeScript with zod? The working expectation is that the checking ladder, presence axes, parse-don’t-validate, functional core / imperative shell, one-canonical-artifact, and the two error channels are fully portable; the specific rungs 2–5 (property classes, property validators, class validators, aggregate roots as S7 mechanisms), dispatch-position abstract parents, and the property-factory stratum are S7’s local realization. Making the tagging explicit would tell a reader which halves of this compendium they are allowed to keep when they change languages — worth a pass if the documents ever get one more edition.

title: Appendix A — Open Questions: The Inquiry Ledger
section: A.8 What evidence would change what
text:
A.8 What evidence would change what
Concrete tripwires, so revisions are triggered by evidence rather than mood:

If S7 gains sealed classes or exhaustiveness checking — retire the registry-driven exhaustiveness tests; simplify the sum-type decision guide.
If S7 gains a load-time revalidation or migration hook — rewrite the object-evolution section; the rds-is-a-cache hypothesis weakens.
If measured validator overhead proves negligible on realistic document graphs — the cost rationale for keeping validators cheap softens; the purity rationale (validators run on every write, so effects would be chaos) stands regardless.
If two or more packages ship generated class graphs with a healthy hand-designed semantic layer on top — soften “generate tables, not class graphs” toward “generate either, but always label the transport stratum.”
If valid_eventually() turns out to be routine in user code rather than rare — reword “construction is the certificate” to lead with the conventional nature of the guarantee, not mention it as a footnote.
If a second MVU-style S7 application appears outside terminal UIs — promote MVU from named variant to recommended architecture for event-driven value cores.
